docs.title: tensor-grep documentation
docs.text: tensor-grep (tg) helps you search text and code, inspect relationships between symbols, and prepare bounded context for a code change. Start with the first-search guide if you are new to the command line.

docs.title: Choose a task
docs.text:
• Find words or a pattern in logs and files: Getting started.
  • Find code by its structure, such as a function call: AST search.
  • See likely important files or gather context for a change: Orientation and context.
  • Reuse a project snapshot across requests: Sessions.
  • Save and restore one file during an edit: Checkpoints.
  • Install tg or check platform support: Installation and support matrix.

docs.title: Use and integration
docs.text:
• Experimental features describes optional features, their setup, and limits.
  • Cache management distinguishes search indexes, AST data, sessions, and checkpoints.
  • Harness cookbook gives task examples for AI and editor integrations.
  • Harness API documents the CLI and MCP machine-readable interfaces; session daemon covers repeated session requests.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Architecture maps the Rust and Python entry points, search engines, caches, and source directories. For the maintained search-routing rules, see routing policy. For compatibility promises, see contracts.

docs.title: Maintainers and operators
docs.text:
• Benchmarks records accepted comparisons and their limits.
  • Tool comparison describes workload-specific strengths and limits.
  • CI pipeline, release checklist, and package publishing cover delivery.
  • Hotfix procedure and enterprise review bundle cover operational workflows.
  • GPU troubleshooting and resident worker runbook cover optional paths.

docs.title: CI Pipeline
docs.text:
tensor-grep treats CI as part of the product contract, not a best-effort test runner. If you change workflow behavior, release behavior, package-manager behavior, or supply-chain automation, update the validator-backed tests in scripts/validate_release_assets.py and tests/unit/test_release_assets_validation_*.py.

Release/package parity validation now includes the editable tensor-grep version recorded in uv.lock, not just pyproject.toml, rust_core/Cargo.toml, and npm/package.json. The semantic-release build command must refresh that lock entry with uv lock --upgrade-package tensor-grep and stage uv.lock before building artifacts.

docs.title: ci.yml
docs.text:
Runs on pushes to main, pull requests targeting main, and a weekly schedule.

Primary responsibilities:

  • release-readiness: strict docs build plus workflow/package-manager validator checks
  • Formatting & Linting: Rust formatting/clippy plus Python Ruff and mypy
  • test-python: cross-platform Python test matrix
  • test-rust-core: cross-platform Rust test matrix
  • search-golden-parity: Windows routing parity guard
  • native-build-smoke: native binary smoke tests across platforms, including both macos-latest (arm64) and macos-15-intel (x86_64) so PR CI matches the Intel release asset built for tg-macos-amd64-cpu
  • package-manager-readiness: Homebrew/Winget/package-manager bundle validation
  • benchmark-regression: blocking same-runner base-vs-head regression gate plus accepted-baseline drift reporting
  • Semantic Release: semantic-release on main
  • build-release-native-assets: builds release-native CPU front doors from the semantic-release tag when steps.release.outputs.released == 'true'; the macOS amd64 asset is built on an Intel macOS runner label. The default release-native asset profile remains CPU-only native-frontdoor. Setting repository variable TENSOR_GREP_RELEASE_NATIVE_ASSET_PROFILE=native-frontdoor-gpu additionally enables opt-in Linux/Windows NVIDIA front-door assets built with CUDA features.
  • publish-github-release-assets: uploads and verifies GitHub release assets for the semantic-release tag when steps.release.outputs.released == 'true'
  • PyPI build, validation, and publish jobs when semantic-release emits a new version. Wheel and sdist jobs prefetch Rust dependencies with a longer Cargo retry window before maturin so transient crates.io DNS failures do not prematurely cancel publication.

Release behavior:

  • Conventional commit subjects drive semantic-release intent.
  • feat: => minor
  • fix: / perf: => patch
  • feat!: / fix!: => major
  • docs: / test: / ci: / chore: / build: => no package release
  • A branch push or open PR starts PR CI only. It is not a release, not a released version, and not complete release state.
  • Release versioning starts only after a release-bearing PR is squash-merged to main, because semantic-release reads the final main commit subject.
  • Release completion requires main CI and semantic-release complete successfully, GitHub release native asset upload/verification passing for the semantic-release tag, publish-success-gate passing when publish is required, git fetch origin main --tags, local main fast-forwarded to the release commit, and PyPI/public installer availability verified when the install/update path changed.

Benchmark behavior:

  • Pull requests benchmark the candidate checkout and the PR base revision in the same runner job; the explicit base-vs-head comparison is the blocking regression gate.
  • Pushes to main benchmark the current checkout and ${{ github.event.before }} in the same runner job; that explicit comparison is the blocking regression gate before semantic-release.
  • Scheduled runs keep accepted-baseline drift reporting and summary generation, but do not block on a synthetic base-vs-head comparison.
  • Accepted baseline JSONs remain the public benchmark truth surface, but drift against them is reported separately from the release-blocking same-runner comparison.

docs.title: release.yml
docs.text: Manual/backfill release artifact pipeline, dispatched via workflow_dispatch TARGETING a published tag ref (gh workflow run release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z; GITHUB_REF then resolves to that tag). It is NOT triggered by a tag push, so a manually-pushed v* tag can no longer bypass semantic-release to auto-publish npm/assets. Do not rely on it for the normal semantic-release path. The authoritative release-bearing path is now ci.yml on main: semantic-release creates the tag/release, main CI checks the action's released output, builds release-native CPU front-door assets from that tag, uploads them to the GitHub release, verifies checksum/package-manager coverage, then allows PyPI publish and publish-success-gate to complete.

docs.title: benchmark.yml (Benchmarks)
docs.text:
Runs the standalone benchmark workflow on a schedule and via manual dispatch.

Primary responsibilities:

  • run benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py and benchmarks/run_ast_benchmarks.py
  • provision AST benchmark prerequisites before the suite: ripgrep, hyperfine, ast-grep, and a freshly built native release tg binary
  • optionally run benchmarks/run_gpu_benchmarks.py on manual dispatch
  • perform the OS-baseline regression check when a stored baseline exists
  • publish the benchmark markdown summary and artifacts

This workflow is not the release-blocking same-runner regression gate from ci.yml; it is the canonical scheduled/manual benchmark automation surface and should stay documented and validator-backed.

docs.title: public-gpu-proof.yml
docs.text:
Manual-only workflow for public managed NVIDIA GPU promotion proof. It is intentionally not part of normal PR, push, or scheduled CI because it requires a fixed GPU-capable runner label: self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu, and tensor-grep-public-gpu-proof. The job targets environment: public-gpu-proof so repository maintainers can require explicit approval before dispatching unattended promotion proof on the self-hosted GPU runner.

The workflow validates a vX.Y.Z release tag, checks out that tag, verifies GitHub release assets with --expected-profile native-frontdoor-gpu, installs the requested public release with TENSOR_GREP_NATIVE_FRONTDOOR_FLAVOR=nvidia, records nvidia-smi and tg doctor --json, then runs:

uv run python benchmarks/run_gpu_native_benchmarks.py \
  --binary "$HOME/.tensor-grep/bin/tg" \
  --corpus-sizes 1GB,5GB \
  --advanced \
  --public-managed-proof

The artifact is promotion-quality only when the benchmark emits public_gpu_proof = true and public_managed_promotion_ready = true. That public gate requires managed NVIDIA front-door metadata, NativeGpuBackend with sidecar_used = false, direct rg --json 1GB/5GB route and correctness evidence, and the advanced many fixed-string proof gate against the fair single-invocation rg -F -e ... -e ... baseline. Local CUDA-feature binaries, sidecar rows, CPU fallback rows, or single-pattern speed wins remain implementation evidence, not public managed acceleration proof.

docs.title: audit.yml
docs.text:
Runs dependency and license audits:

  • cargo audit
  • cargo deny check
  • pip-audit

The Python audit exports the fully locked uv.lock dependency graph to a hashed requirements file under $RUNNER_TEMP, then runs pip-audit with --require-hashes and --disable-pip against that file. This keeps the scanner/runtime environment out of the audited dependency set, while still checking all extras from the resolved lock. The repo also owns pyproject.toml tool.uv.constraint-dependencies security floors for audited transitive packages. When pip-audit reports a vulnerable transitive dependency, update those constraints, refresh uv.lock, and extend the validator-backed tests instead of silently pinning the package as a new top-level runtime dependency. The validator also treats pytest>=9.0.3 in both dev and bench extras as audit parity surface, because those extras are included in the locked Python audit graph. Formatter parity also depends on an exact Ruff dev pin. CI runs Ruff in preview mode, and Ruff's versioning allows formatter behavior to change across releases, so keep the repo-owned ruff==0.15.11 pin and the validator tests in sync when intentionally upgrading the formatter. Operationally, local release gates must run both uv run ruff check . and uv run ruff format --check --preview .. A non-preview local format pass is not sufficient, because preview formatting can reflow files differently and fail the Formatting & Linting job after push.

The Rust license policy for cargo deny check is owned in-repo at rust_core/deny.toml. If the Rust dependency graph changes, update that policy and the audit workflow contract tests together rather than relying on cargo-deny defaults.

Triggers:

  • nightly schedule
  • pull requests to main
  • manual dispatch

On the nightly scheduled run only:

  • if the audit fails, CI creates or updates a single tracked GitHub issue: [Security Audit] Scheduled dependency audit failure
  • if the next nightly audit succeeds, CI closes that issue automatically

This closes the loop from detection to owned remediation instead of silently failing in Actions history.

docs.title: Dependabot Maintenance
docs.text:
Dependabot is configured in .github/dependabot.yml for:

  • github-actions
  • uv
  • cargo
  • npm

The automation workflow .github/workflows/dependabot-automation.yml applies labels, triages update risk, and enables auto-merge only for low-risk updates:

  • patch/minor GitHub Actions updates
  • patch/minor non-production (direct:development) or indirect dependency updates

The Dependabot automation workflow intentionally runs without a checkout step. Every gh CLI call in that workflow must target the repository explicitly via job-level GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }} and --repo "$GH_REPO" on each command, or label/PR automation will fail outside a git worktree.

It does not auto-merge:

  • semver-major updates
  • direct production/runtime dependency updates

Those remain manual-review changes.

docs.title: Changing workflows
docs.text:
If you touch .github/workflows/*.yml, .github/dependabot.yml, or release/package-manager behavior:

  1. update the workflow/config
  2. update scripts/validate_release_assets.py
  3. update tests/unit/test_release_assets_validation_*.py
  4. run:
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check --preview .
uv run mypy src/tensor_grep
uv run pytest -q
uv run python scripts/validate_release_assets.py

CI behavior is a versioned contract; update its documentation and validation with the workflow.

After a release-bearing push to main, semantic-release may create and push a follow-up chore(release): vX.Y.Z [skip ci] commit that updates CHANGELOG.md, version files, package manager manifests, and uv.lock. Operators and agents must fetch tags/main and fast-forward the local checkout before checking version files or declaring the release complete.

The same release is incomplete until publish-github-release-assets verifies the installer-critical GitHub assets for the selected profile. The default native-frontdoor profile requires tg-linux-amd64-cpu, tg-macos-amd64-cpu, tg-windows-amd64-cpu.exe, CHECKSUMS.txt, and package-manager bundle files. The opt-in native-frontdoor-gpu profile additionally requires tg-linux-amd64-nvidia and tg-windows-amd64-nvidia.exe; macOS remains CPU-only. The macOS amd64 asset must be built on an Intel macOS runner, currently macos-15-intel; macos-latest is arm64. PyPI visibility alone is not enough evidence when installer or package-manager URLs depend on GitHub release assets. Non-release main pushes must leave the semantic-release version output empty so these asset jobs do not mutate an older GitHub release.

docs.title: Conditional PR jobs
docs.text: A changes job computes whether a pull_request's diff touches CODE (src/, rust_core/, tests/, .github/workflows/, pyproject.toml, Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, uv.lock). The expensive/cross-platform jobs (agent-readiness, windows-agent-readiness, static-analysis, test-python, test-rust-core, cuda-feature-check, search-golden-parity, native-build-smoke, test-gpu-linux, benchmark-regression) gate on if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' || needs.changes.outputs.code == 'true'. - MAIN pushes always run the full matrix, so release (which needs: them) is never skipped. - A docs-only PR skips those jobs; a skipped required job counts as SUCCESS for branch protection (never use trigger-level paths-ignore — no status => deadlock). - test-rust-core drops the macOS x nightly leg (nightly still runs on Linux/Windows; consult the workflow for the current channel matrix). - Gated jobs declare needs: [smoke, changes]; the smoke gate is still enforced (see the release-workflow-configuration validator).

docs.title: API and Data Contracts
docs.text:
This document defines the backward-compatibility guarantees for data structures and CLI outputs used by enterprise integrations, IDEs, and editor-plane agents.

release_docs_current_tag: v1.124.0

docs.title: 0. The completeness contract (governs every section below)
docs.text:
Every tg answer is either complete, or it names exactly how it is incomplete and whether the caller can do anything about it.

This is the one promise the rest of this document implements. It exists because tg's primary caller is an AI agent, and an agent cannot tell a genuinely empty result from a silently truncated one. "No callers found" acted on in good faith deletes working code. A result that is smaller than the question it claims to answer, with no marker saying so, is a wrong answer -- not a smaller one.

Three obligations follow, in priority order:

  • P1 -- no silent loss. A command that drops an entry it could not read must say so. Never return a shortened collection with a success marker. Where dropping the entry would corrupt the answer rather than shrink it, fail closed instead: refuse, and leave the caller's state untouched.
  • P2 -- actionable disclosure. Naming the incompleteness is not enough; the caller needs to know whether it is theirs to fix. A budget cause (scan_limit, deadline) is remediable -- raise the knob. An unreadable path is not: no budget increase makes it readable. Handing over the wrong knob is its own defect class, and the reason unreadable_path OUTRANKS every budget cause when both fire.
  • P3 -- surface agreement. The CLI, the --json envelope, the exit code and the MCP tools must tell the same story about the same run. A renderer must never change the answer.

docs.title: 1. Configuration (sgconfig.yml)
docs.text: The root-level keys and structure of sgconfig.yml are guaranteed to be stable within a major version. Unrecognized keys will be ignored rather than causing fatal errors to allow progressive rollout of new configurations.

docs.title: 2. AST Cache (project_data_v6.json)
docs.text: The schema of the .tg_cache/ast/project_data_v6.json cache is versioned within its filename. - Backward compatibility is NOT guaranteed across major/minor versions. - If the schema changes (for example to v7), tensor-grep will automatically invalidate older cache files and rebuild them transparently.

docs.title: 3. Text-search compatibility
docs.text:
The stable text-search compatibility contract is the validated compatibility set covered by the parity suite and contract benchmark runner. tg search --help may expose more rg-style flags, but only the rows below and explicitly named deterministic edges are part of the public rg-compatibility claim.

Current validated rows: - -i/--ignore-case - -v/--invert-match - -C/--context - -A/--after-context - -B/--before-context - -g/--glob - -l/--files-with-matches - --files-without-match - tensor-grep aggregate --json - ripgrep JSON Lines via explicit --format rg --json - --ndjson - -F/--fixed-strings - -w/--word-regexp - -m/--max-count - --files - -t/--type - -./--hidden - -L/--follow - -S/--smart-case - -n/--line-number - --column - -c/--count - --count-matches - -a/--text - -0/--null - -U/--multiline - --multiline-dotall

Character-for-character identity is not required for help formatting, but command presence, supported rows, accepted normalization, and the deterministic parity corpus are part of the public contract. Additional rg-style flags may be exposed in tg search --help, but they are not covered by the stable compatibility claim until they are added to the contract suite and benchmark runner.

Agent automation contracts: - tg search PATTERN defaults to the current directory when no path is provided. - Invalid regex syntax exits as an error distinct from no-match and emits a diagnostic that recommends --fixed-strings for literal searches. - tg search --json emits a valid tensor-grep aggregate JSON object even when there are zero matches. - tg search --format rg --json forwards to ripgrep and emits rg JSON Lines events without a tensor-grep envelope for tools that require rg's event schema. - tg search --files-with-matches stays root-based on the ripgrep path instead of expanding large candidate-file lists into the Windows process argument vector, and plain path-list output emits one trailing line separator only. - tg search with --format rg is a public exact ripgrep-style text formatter for automation that needs rg-shaped stdout. Pair it with --sort path when deterministic path ordering matters across backends. - The native front door treats --format rg as a no-op for rg-compatible text output and preserves --sort path when forwarding to ripgrep. Non-rg --format search output remains a Python CLI formatting surface. - The public native front door must not reject flags advertised by the public Python CLI. It may execute the request natively, forward to ripgrep, or route to the Python sidecar, but sidecar routing must be intentional and covered by a public-native regression test. - Root shortcut invocations with option-first common search flags, including tg -t js PATTERN PATH and tg --count-matches PATTERN PATH, are treated as tg search ... and must preserve those flags through native, ripgrep, or sidecar routing instead of falling back to positional-only parsing. - Cached-session requests must stay on the warm path by default. One-shot tg session ... commands and daemon-routed session requests validate files captured in the session snapshot with direct size/mtime checks and must not walk the full repository merely to check for added files. Added-file discovery belongs to explicit refresh paths: tg session refresh ... and requests that opt into --refresh-on-stale. A session opened on a repo with zero context files is still subject to added-file detection on those explicit paths. Daemon response-cache hits intentionally use detect_added_files=False before serving cached context-render / edit-plan payloads so truncated implicit sessions stay fast; new files under the repo are invisible to response-cache invalidation until refresh_on_stale or tg session refresh. Daemon stats exposes response_cache_stale_detection = "snapshot_mtime_only" and response_cache_added_file_detection = false so agents can see the tradeoff without guessing. The 5 symbol commands (defs / impact / refs / callers / blast-radius) are also response-cached: a repeated warm request with an identical symbol/provider/max-tests/max-depth/max-repo-files is served straight from the daemon's response cache instead of re-running the caller-scan or blast-radius graph walk. Unlike context-render / edit-plan, the symbol-command gate honors the request's real refresh_on_stale flag -- added-file detection included -- before trusting a cache hit, because a caller/blast-radius answer that silently omits a newly-added call site is a wrong answer, not merely a stale one; a genuinely new file (or a modified/removed tracked file) busts a symbol-command cache entry on the very next request. Session edit-plan graph ranking, test matching, and blast-radius metadata must stay bounded to selected context budgets and report the bounded radius scope in edit_plan_seed.blast_radius_scope; daemon requests should keep a short connect probe while allowing longer edit-plan/context responses. Top-level native-provider tg context-render and tg edit-plan may reuse an already-running daemon and create an implicit session keyed by root and max_repo_files so repeated agent-loop calls hit daemon response-cache counters without reusing a smaller scan budget for later larger requests. tg session list and tg session daemon status should discover nearby session scopes when the requested/current root has no direct session metadata, and JSON output should expose whether discovery was used. Daemon-routed relative paths are resolved against the daemon root before session lookup so tg session edit-plan ID . --daemon works from the served project root and does not accidentally target the daemon process working directory. - tg checkpoint list PATH must keep default discovery nearby and bounded: direct scope, ancestors, and immediate non-generated children only when the direct scope is empty. Recursive child-scope discovery is opt-in through --discover; generated/cache roots require the explicit --discover-full mode. Explicit recursive discovery may cache fingerprinted checkpoint index paths for repeat calls, but create and undo must invalidate ancestor discovery caches so agent loops do not reuse stale scope lists after checkpoint state changes. - tg search --files remains a generated-root guardrail surface. The native front door may route it to the Python sidecar so broad generated-root refusal, --glob, --type, --max-depth, and --allow-broad-generated-scan keep the same public semantics. - tg search --multiline / -U, --multiline-dotall, and -0/--null must be accepted by the native front door and forwarded to the backend that preserves rg-compatible behavior for the requested output mode. - --sort path is the deterministic contract for --files-with-matches, --files-without-match, --replace, and path-list automation. The parity suite also checks match, no-match, parse-error, and binary-skip exit-code behavior. - Default output ordering for root-scale --files-with-matches, --count, and --force-cpu is a semantic result parity contract, not a golden stdout ordering contract. Use --sort path when automation needs deterministic path ordering across backends. - Broad generated roots such as .claude are routed through Python guardrails instead of rust-first/native passthrough so generated .claude/context snapshots can be pruned by default. - Unbounded broad generated-root scan requests are refused with exit code 2 when hidden file-list scans contain generated, cache, or dependency child directories, or when content searches directly target a generated/cache/dependency root. Explicit --no-ignore content searches over an ordinary project root follow ripgrep and may traverse ignored generated child directories; direct generated roots still require a scoped path, --glob, --type, --max-depth, or --allow-broad-generated-scan. Unbounded searches against a parent that looks like a multi-project workspace root are also refused before the broad walk. tg scan / MCP ruleset scans apply the same safety posture to AST/ruleset workflows: direct temp, AppData, user-home, filesystem-root, generated/cache/dependency, or multi-project workspace roots must be scoped to a project/subdirectory, bounded with --max-depth (and optionally --glob / --type), or explicitly opted in with --allow-broad-generated-scan before any scanner walk begins. - tg search honors a root .ignore/.gitignore/.rgignore uniformly, including in a non-git directory, where raw rg's own require_git default makes an un-flagged .gitignore inert. This is a deliberate, permanent divergence from raw rg in that one cell, not an unintended parity gap: --no-ignore and --no-ignore-vcs opt back out, matching rg's own documented per-flag scope. - An implicit-path tg search (PATH omitted, defaulting to the current directory per the earlier bullet) whose directory WALK exceeds an internal file-count ceiling (1500 files visited, counted independent of match count or glob/type selectivity) is refused with exit code 2 and an actionable message instead of running unbounded. This guard runs as the first statement of execute_ripgrep_search itself, so it applies uniformly across every entry point that can reach that function -- the full Python CLI, the standalone native binary's default search front door (including its -e/--regexp form), the positional CLI, tg-search-fast, and the PyO3 FFI bridge -- rather than one call site that a different entry point could bypass. An explicit, deliberately-scoped PATH is never refused regardless of size. - tg search --type-list prints a built-in fallback list when no ripgrep or standalone native binary is available. --pcre2-version follows ripgrep semantics and exits with an error when no PCRE2-capable backend is available. - tg ast-info --json exposes AST language identifiers via {"languages": [...]} for agent discovery without help-text scraping. - Read-only tg run follows search-style no-match semantics: zero AST matches exit 1 while successful matches exit 0; parse/configuration errors remain distinct non-zero failures. On Windows, if the received pattern is still wrapped in single quotes, tg run warns that cmd.exe treats those quotes literally and suggests double quotes for cmd.exe. - Native exit-code honesty: 0 found, 1 genuinely no match, 2 error or incomplete. A child process (ripgrep, the Python sidecar) that is killed by a signal or crashes with a negative NTSTATUS exits 2, never 1; tg run command errors (for example Path not found) and --index search failures exit 2; a --apply that fails part-way exits 2 and its error lists files_written and files_failed (written files are NOT rolled back, and a failed file may be partially modified). --index decodes non-UTF-8 files lossily (U+FFFD in match text) instead of aborting the search. -c/--count combined with --json or --ndjson now emits only the normal structured payload (with match_counts_by_file) instead of plain path:count lines mixed into JSON; this is a payload-size increase for count users. The did-you-mean nearest[] list is ranked by edit distance (closest first, alphabetical tie-break) BEFORE the cap of 5 in both front doors. - On Windows, PowerShell automation should invoke tg or tg.ps1 for regex metacharacters. PowerShell double quotes expand $NAME-style values before tensor-grep receives argv, so literal patterns containing $ should use single quotes or escape $ as `$. Direct .cmd invocation from PowerShell is not a safe argv-preserving contract for unescaped metacharacters such as | because cmd.exe parses the line before the batch wrapper receives arguments; tg.cmd is for cmd.exe. - The quoted multi-word no-match pattern case from cmd.exe, direct tg.cmd, and Python subprocess.run([...]) is a public launcher contract. The launcher must preserve the phrase as one argv item and must not turn it into a shorter false-positive search plus bogus paths. - Stable managed install scripts should prefer the matching release-native CPU tg binary as the public front door when the GitHub release asset is available, set TG_SIDECAR_PYTHON for Python-backed commands, set TG_NATIVE_TG_BINARY for the sidecar, and fall back to python -m tensor_grep when no native asset exists. On Windows, the managed native front-door directory must be placed on User PATH ahead of compatibility shim directories so cmd, unprofiled PowerShell, and subprocess.run(["tg", ...]) resolve ~/.tensor-grep/bin/tg.exe before the slower argv-safe tg.cmd bridge. If a tensor-grep-owned tg.com bridge is copied into another PATH directory to outrank a foreign same-directory tg.exe, the bridge must still find ~/.tensor-grep/.venv for sidecar-backed commands and must point TG_NATIVE_TG_BINARY back at the managed front door rather than the bridge copy. - tg doctor --json must make launcher routing observable. It should report path_tg_first_launcher_kind for the current process PATH, fresh_shell_path_tg_first_launcher_kind for Windows fresh-shell PATH when available, python_subprocess_path_tg_first_launcher_kind for Python subprocess.run(["tg", ...]) style resolution, and path_tg_launcher_warning when the current process still resolves a compatibility shim even though a fresh shell would resolve the managed native front door. It also exposes shell_escaping_guidance so automation can surface PowerShell $ expansion and cmd.exe metacharacter escaping guidance without scraping README prose. This warning is diagnostic: it means restart or refresh PATH before timing subprocess-heavy workflows. Python subprocess resolution is its own contract because Windows CreateProcess can choose a foreign same-directory tg.exe even when shells prefer a tensor-grep tg.com bridge through PATHEXT. - tg doctor --json must also make GPU search routing observable. gpu.search_runtime_probe should run a small fixed-string tg search --gpu-device-ids ... --json probe through the resolved native front door and report requested_gpu_device_ids, routing_backend, routing_reason, sidecar_used, routing_gpu_device_ids, and a status that is supported only for NativeGpuBackend with sidecar_used = false. - If the first PATH or Python-subprocess tg reports a version string that is not tensor-grep-shaped (tg ... or tensor-grep ...), tg doctor --json should classify it as foreign, set path_tg_first_is_foreign, fresh_shell_path_tg_first_is_foreign, or python_subprocess_path_tg_first_is_foreign, and emit a warning plus remediation field such as path_tg_foreign_warning, path_tg_foreign_remediation, fresh_shell_path_tg_foreign_warning, fresh_shell_path_tg_foreign_remediation, python_subprocess_path_tg_foreign_warning, and python_subprocess_path_tg_foreign_remediation. Foreign launchers are not tensor-grep-owned stale launchers: readiness should fail with explicit remediation, and installer/doctor code must not delete or overwrite unrelated tools. The explicit repair path is tg repair-launcher: it removes verified tensor-grep-owned Python Scripts entrypoints and backs up self-identifying orphaned tensor-grep Python Scripts entrypoints that shadow the managed native front door. With --allow-foreign-rename, it is Windows-only, backs up the first foreign Python-subprocess tg.exe to a .bak file, installs the verified managed native front door into that same PATH slot, and must refuse to act on a foreign launcher without the allow flag. - Stable installers must build replacement managed environments and front-door files in a staging directory and only swap them into ~/.tensor-grep after package installation and front-door generation succeed. PowerShell installer native commands must check $LASTEXITCODE before the staged swap. A failed package resolve/install must preserve the previous managed install and shims. - tg upgrade must not infer "latest PyPI version" solely from unchanged local metadata. It should refresh package metadata, skip yanked PyPI releases when selecting an exact version, pin the latest same-or-newer PyPI version when known, verify the target Python can import tensor_grep, and report a verification error instead of success if the sidecar is corrupted. The scheduled Windows self-upgrade helper must run the same import/version verification before writing a success log. When the underlying repo scan was truncated, the capsule additively carries the same scan-side fields the other code-intelligence commands expose — scan_limit, scan_remediation, partial, partial_reason, deadline_limit, and result_incomplete — only when present; a pure render/token output cap on the capsule's own snippet budget never sets these. partial_reason is currently always "deadline" when present on agent/context/context-render/edit-plan output (mirrors tg codemap's own partial_reason field, which additionally distinguishes "scan_limit"/"self_verify"/"unreadable_path" for its own coverage contract -- and note "unreadable_path" is the ONE value in that set that is NOT budget-remediable: "scan_limit" and "deadline" are both answered by raising a limit, but no --max-repo-files or --deadline value makes a permission-denied subtree readable, so tg codemap's remediation string says so explicitly and, when a budget cause fires alongside it, names the budget knob while stating that raising it still leaves the hole. Do NOT read this list as closed against future causes -- it is the set wired so far): partial = true on these four commands is a strictly time-budget signal, so a partial_reason = "deadline" payload can be substantively complete and correct — every stage that ran found everything it looked for — but still reports partial because SOME stage, checkpointed or not, pushed total elapsed time past the caller's --deadline before the payload returned. This is a deliberate false-partial: each command's builder rechecks the shared absolute deadline one final time at its own return point (regardless of which internal stage actually consumed the time) and would rather flag a technically-complete-but-late response as partial than silently report exit 0 on a response that blew its declared time budget. partial_reason = "deadline" is therefore NOT the same signal as result_incomplete (which means data was actually dropped by a --max-repo-files / count cap) — a payload can be partial with partial_reason = "deadline" and NOT result_incomplete, or vice versa, or both at once. - When tg agent's deadline_limit is present (per the false-partial rationale above), it additively carries assembly_stages_skipped — a list naming which POST-collection ASSEMBLY stage(s) (currently "vendored_subtree_detection", "suggested_scope", "context_pack_assembly") were skipped because the shared --deadline budget was already exhausted by the time that stage would have started. An OUTPUT-only cap (output_limit.possibly_truncated from --max-files on map, or --max-callers/--max-files render caps) is a COMPLETE analysis capped only for display and stays exit 0; only a SCAN truncation exits 2.

  • --deadline is additionally accepted on the true symbol commands tg source and tg blast-radius-plan follows the same three-state exit contract as defs/impact/refs/callers/blast-radius; both thread deadline_seconds into build_symbol_source/build_symbol_blast_radius_plan the same additive way (build_repo_map's existing deadline_monotonic parameter), so a truncated scan now correctly surfaces partial/deadline_limit and exits 2 on both. It is also accepted on tg docs-coverage (both the default coverage report and --stale mode): a --deadline-caused walk truncation is a NEW, separate signal from the command's pre-existing --max-repo-files count-cap (scan_limit.possibly_truncated with truncation_cause: "project-files", unchanged, still exits 0 — raising the cap is a real remedy, so the caller can always fix it and the field alone suffices) — the partial/deadline_limit time-budget signal exits 2, checked before --check's own exit-1 gate so truncation trumps a (possibly wrong) confident coverage/stale count, mirroring the found-vs-truncated precedent above. scan_limit.truncation_cause is a CLOSED VOCABULARY. tg inventory --json and tg docs-coverage --json expose exactly three values, and an agent branches on the string to decide whether retrying is worthwhile: project-files — the --max-files/--max-repo-files count cap, BUDGET-REMEDIABLE, raise it; deadline — the --deadline wall-clock bound, BUDGET-REMEDIABLE, raise it; unreadable-path — the walk, or a per-file read/stat inside it, hit a path it could not read, and this one is NOT budget-remediable: no cap or deadline value makes a permission-denied path readable, so the correct response is to make the path readable or scope the request away from it, never a bigger budget. An unrecognised value must never be treated as budget-remediable (the fail-closed allow-list rule). NOTE this field is DISTINCT from incomplete_reason_class/partial_reason documented above, which the search and codemap routes carry with an UNDERSCORED vocabulary (scan_limit/deadline/timeout/unreadable_path). The two spellings are deliberate and each is internally consistent within its own field — truncation_cause's siblings are hyphenated, incomplete_reason_class's are not. Do NOT "unify" them: renaming either breaks a documented contract for no correctness gain. truncation_cause: "unreadable-path" also exits 2; the "project-files" budget-cap contract stays exit 0. tg imports also accepts --deadline but is a documented NO-OP: it resolves a single file's own imports (O(1), no repo scan to bound), so the flag exists solely so an agent that learned --deadline works elsewhere does not get a Click "No such option" exit-2 here; the value is never threaded anywhere and output is byte-identical with or without it.

  • budget_remediable on the CLI scan_limit/output_limit objects. The remediability distinction the MCP tg_search surface has carried since contract 1.5.0 (see the MCP bullet below) is now also emitted CLI-side, so a caller does not have to re-derive it from the cause string. It appears on tg inventory, tg docs-coverage, and the shared repo-map payloads (tg map, tg session open/show/refresh) — additively, and ONLY when a cause is present, so a COMPLETE scan emits neither field and stays byte-identical to before. Its value is derived from the ONE shared allow-list in src/tensor_grep/cli/incompleteness.py::budget_remediable, never re-implemented per surface, because two copies is how CLI and MCP drift into giving opposite advice for the same cause. It is gated on whether a cause exists, NOT on possibly_truncated: in the repo-map payloads possibly_truncated is deliberately narrow (true only for dropped project files), so gating there would omit the flag for an unreadable-path cap — withholding budget_remediable: false when a larger budget cannot fix the cause, which would give the caller incorrect retry advice. output_limit is the one surface where truncated and capped are the same condition; its value is still derived from the cause rather than hardcoded, so a future cause cannot silently inherit "just raise the limit".
  • tg orient and tg agent join the warm-session-daemon fast path (TG_SESSION_DAEMON_AUTOSTART, default ON; no separate flag) via orient/agent daemon commands, build_orient_capsule_from_map/build_agent_capsule_from_map, and dedicated response-cache key builders (_orient_response_cache_key/_agent_response_cache_key) that key on every output-affecting flag, mirroring the 5 symbol commands' anti-bleed discipline. Both are added-file-sensitive: an implicit session honors the caller's refresh_on_stale for added-file detection, not the context-render/edit-plan detect_added_files=False shortcut, because a new central file (orient) or a new call site (agent) changes the answer, not just its staleness. Warm answers must preserve these correctness checks: TRAP A — agent's call-site-evidence collector runs build_symbol_blast_radius_from_map against the daemon's cached map, which has no literal-seed rescue (unlike the cold build_symbol_blast_radius wrapper, which retries via _literal_symbol_seed_files on a truncated no_match); when that condition fires, the response carries an internal daemon_evidence_unreliable: true sentinel and the client (main._maybe_agent_via_running_daemon) discards the whole response and falls back to cold instead of serving call-site evidence it cannot trust. TRAP B — suggested_scope is computed in the build_context_render WRAPPER (not build_context_render_from_map); build_agent_capsule_from_map replicates that exact block against its own map so a warm capsule does not silently drop suggested_scope on a truncated scan. --gpu-device-ids on tg agent never routes to the daemon (the GPU evidence probe shells out to a fresh tg search subprocess, which must not run inside a daemon worker thread) — it always takes the cold path.
  • --deadline on the cold path of tg agent, tg context-render, tg edit-plan, tg orient, and tg codemap is measured from CLI command entry, not just the underlying repo scan: main.py's _cli_deadline_monotonic anchors the absolute time.monotonic() deadline at the TOP of the command body — before the lazy builder import, path/query resolution, GPU-id parsing, and the warm-daemon-skip gate — so that front-door time is budgeted the same way scan time already is. The five cold-path builders (build_agent_capsule, build_context_render, build_context_edit_plan, build_orient_capsule, build_codemap) accept an optional pre-anchored deadline_monotonic override that takes precedence over recomputing a fresh one from deadline_seconds; direct callers that only pass deadline_seconds (the MCP tool, the session daemon's own _from_map variants, tests) are unaffected — the fallback computation is byte-identical to the prior behavior. tg agent's own separate cold-path-only default (DEFAULT_AGENT_CLI_DEADLINE_SECONDS, applied only when neither --deadline nor --no-deadline is passed) is unaffected by this fix and keeps its existing anchor point, computed after the daemon-miss decision — that generous default bound is not the small-explicit---deadline case this fix targets. The remaining process-startup prefix — interpreter boot plus Typer/Click argument dispatch, which runs before Python even reaches the command body — is a separate startup interval that no CLI command body can account for; it is not included in any --deadline budget.
  • tg route-test runs the FULL context-render AND edit-plan builds back to back to compare their primary targets, so — unlike context-render/edit-plan themselves, which stay unbounded by default — it is the one command in this family with a cold-only DEFAULT --deadline bound: it reuses DEFAULT_AGENT_CLI_DEADLINE_SECONDS (tg agent's existing 60s cold-path constant) rather than inventing a second default, because the composite cost was observed overrunning an external harness's own timeout under concurrent load even though a single side alone finished well inside it. Both builder calls share ONE pre-anchored deadline_monotonic (anchored at CLI command entry, before path/query resolution) — side 2 (edit-plan) naturally receives whatever wall-clock side 1 (context-render) left rather than each side getting its own fresh budget. --no-deadline disables the bound entirely; an explicit --deadline overrides the default. Honesty: when EITHER side's builder payload stamps its own partial (a deadline truncation), route-test's composite JSON additively stamps top-level partial: true, partial_reason: "deadline", deadline_limit ({deadline_exceeded, context_render, edit_plan} naming which side(s) truncated), and agreement_basis: "partial" — the tell that the reported agreement boolean was computed from one or two truncated sides and must not be trusted as a full-confidence verdict just because the two sides happen to still agree — then exits 2 through the same _scan_incomplete gate the sibling commands use. route-test has no warm-daemon fast path (cold-only), and a complete comparison (neither side truncated) omits all four additive fields, staying byte-identical to the pre- payload.
  • tg prepare is a thin composition over tg agent's existing capsule builder, not new ranking/scan logic: ONE build_agent_capsule call supplies primary_target, confidence, ask_user_before_editing, validation_plan, and validation_commands verbatim, plus a NEW blast_radius_floor ({symbol, callers_count, top_callers, source, graph_trust_summary, resolution_gaps, possibly_incomplete}) that closes a real gap in the capsule's own call-site collector: _collect_capsule_call_site_evidence only collects when the query names the primary symbol AND its pre-cap confidence is >=0.75, so a natural-language task query leaves it empty even when the SELECTED primary target has real callers. prepare reuses the capsule's own call-site evidence when it already ran (blast_radius_floor.source = "capsule_call_site_evidence"); otherwise it runs exactly ONE supplementary FS-backed scan through the literal-seed-rescue-equipped build_symbol_blast_radius (never the rescue-less _from_map sibling, whose no_match on a possibly-truncated map is a false-complete absence, not a proof the symbol has no callers) keyed on the symbol the capsule actually selected, not the raw query text (source = "supplementary_blast_radius"). prepare additionally emits coordination.claim (a tg ledger claim command preview) and coordination.evidence (a tg evidence emit command preview, since prepare does not itself persist a capsule file to pass as --capsule); the claim is EMIT-ARGS-ONLY by default (submitted: false, no .tensor-grep/ledger write) and only actually calls ledger_store.submit_claim — a claim failure is caught and reported inline, never raised, matching submit_claim's own "never blocks" contract one level up — when --claim is passed. Like route-test, prepare has no warm-daemon fast path and defaults its cold-only --deadline to DEFAULT_AGENT_CLI_DEADLINE_SECONDS (60s) rather than running unbounded, sharing ONE pre-anchored deadline_monotonic across both the capsule build and the blast-radius floor scan so the floor naturally receives whatever wall-clock the capsule build left; --no-deadline disables the bound and an explicit --deadline overrides the default. Honesty: when EITHER the capsule or the floor scan reports its own deadline truncation, prepare additively stamps top-level partial: true, partial_reason: "deadline", and deadline_limit ({deadline_exceeded, capsule, blast_radius_floor} naming which side(s) truncated) before printing the full JSON and exiting 2 through the same _scan_incomplete gate the sibling commands use — a plain max_callers OUTPUT cap on the floor (possibly_incomplete true but no deadline cutoff) stays exit 0, mirroring the output-cap-stays-0 contract above; a complete run omits all of the additive fields and stays exit 0.

Known current limitations: - Explicitly opted-in broad generated-root walks can still be expensive. The Python path-list output path and managed Windows launchers force UTF-8, but scope file-list commands to the smallest useful root whenever possible. - Broad generated roots remain agent-hostile when callers opt in to them. Use scoped paths, globs, file types, and --max-depth for tg search before reaching for opt-in; --max-repo-files, --max-callers, and --max-files are code-intelligence command budgets, not tg search flags. - impact SYMBOL is a broader planning signal and can be noisier than blast-radius; use blast-radius for direct symbol impact checks.

docs.title: 4. Machine-readable CLI output (--json and --ndjson)
docs.text:
The JSON schemas emitted by tensor-grep search --json, tensor-grep search --ndjson, and the documented harness/editor-plane flows are considered public APIs. tensor-grep search --format rg --json is a compatibility route for ripgrep's JSON Lines event schema, so consumers should use rg's event contract rather than the tensor-grep envelope for that mode. - Existing fields (for example file, line, match, context) will not be renamed or removed without a major version bump. - New fields may be added in minor versions. - Consumers should ignore unrecognized JSON fields. - result_incomplete: true payloads additively carry incomplete_reason_class alongside the free-text incomplete_reason -- a closed vocabulary ("unreadable_path", "scan_limit", "deadline", "timeout", "workspace_root_refused", "coverage_gap") an agent can branch on WITHOUT string-sniffing the human-readable reason. It is omitted entirely (not null) on a complete result, matching result_incomplete/incomplete_reason's own omit-when-complete convention, so a complete search stays byte-identical. It is present on the two Python-implemented tg search routes that can set result_incomplete: the rg-backend route (rg's own soft per-path exit-2 error, always "unreadable_path"; a timed-out rg subprocess, "timeout") and the Python CPUBackend fallback route reached when native delegation is refused or unavailable -- no compiled native tg binary on the machine, or a flag native delegation does not support (a directory scan that hit an unreadable path, "unreadable_path"; the scanner's own defensive entry-count budget, "scan_limit"; the native per-file wall-clock budget, "timeout"). A multi-project workspace-root refuse (Python CLI _emit_broad_scan_refusal) uses "workspace_root_refused" so agents do not confuse a parent-workspace refuse with a file-cap truncation; other broad-scan ceilings retain "scan_limit". The compiled native/Rust engine also emits these fields. --cpu, --force-cpu, and --json are themselves native-delegation TRIGGERS (bootstrap.py), so on a normal install with the native tg binary present, tg search ... --cpu --json is answered by the compiled Rust front door reporting routing_backend = "NativeCpuBackend". That route counts unreadable entries into SearchStats.walk_errors (native_search.rs, struct SearchStats), declares the triple on struct NativeJsonOutput and stamps it in emit_json_matches (same file), and exits 2 when the count is non-zero in run_native_search_with_optional_rg_fallback (main.rs) -- the same disclosure and the same exit code as rg on the same directory. The serial-walk collector was the last producer without a count channel and now carries one (WalkedFiles, #276 slice B3). - Route support must be established from the documented backend and its envelope contract, not inferred from an absent reason class alone. Compiled single-pattern CPU output uses NativeJsonOutput; multi-pattern -e/-f routes use SearchResultJson and SearchSummaryNdjson; CUDA output uses GpuNativeSearchResultJson and GpuNativeSearchStats::walk_errors. These producers share incomplete_envelope_fields. The route name alone does not distinguish single-pattern and multi-pattern native CPU execution. - resolution_gaps (symbol commands: defs, refs, callers, source, impact, blast-radius*, imports, importers, file-api) lists every file the symbol graph could not fully read or cover. Each entry carries language, reason, files_affected, files_sample (up to 5, root-relative), remediation and affects_completeness in {"never", "when_empty", "always"}. Kinds: no registered extractor / no reverse-import resolver (never), grammar not installed (when_empty), file over TENSOR_GREP_MAX_PARSE_BYTES, Python syntax error (or RecursionError/NUL byte at parse time), unreadable file, and not-valid-UTF-8 (undecodable bytes were replaced) -- all when_empty. A when_empty gap flips result_incomplete (exit 2, incomplete_reason_class: "coverage_gap") ONLY when the answer is EMPTY, because an empty answer is the one case where silence reads as "proven absent"; a non-empty answer keeps exit 0 and discloses the gap. An earlier cause (a scan limit, a deadline, an unreadable path) keeps incomplete_reason/class/remediation; the gap stays listed. blast-radius, blast-radius-render and blast-radius-plan additionally stamp coverage_gap_limit (possibly_truncated, reason, files_sample, remediation) when a gap blocked the answer, which is what their exit-2 gate and banner read. Missing-grammar behavior: a defs/refs/callers lookup whose grammar is missing and whose answer is empty now exits 2 : an empty answer under a missing grammar is unverified, not absent. tg diff-impact adds unparsed_changed_files (changed files whose symbols could not be extracted) and tg search --enrich-ast marks matches in unparseable files with enclosing_symbol_status: "unparsed". - incomplete_reason_class matters because the causes are NOT equally remediable: "scan_limit"/"deadline"/"timeout" are genuinely fixable by raising a budget (--max-repo-files, --deadline, TG_RG_TIMEOUT_SECONDS/TG_DIR_SCAN_MAX_ENTRIES) or narrowing scope; "workspace_root_refused" is remediable by scoping (--glob/--type/--max-depth/explicit path) or --allow-broad-generated-scan, never by raising a file-cap; "unreadable_path" is NOT budget-remediable -- the path needs to become readable, or the search needs to be scoped away from it. See the exit-code bullet below for the same distinction applied to tg search's exit-2 retry guidance. - The MCP tg_search tool exposes the SAME remediability distinction on its own scan_limit object, from contract version 1.5.0. When -- and only when -- the scan was actually truncated it additively carries truncation_cause ("scan_limit" / "unreadable_path" / "unknown"), budget_remediable (bool), and, when non-zero, unreadable_path_count. A complete scan emits none of them and stays byte-identical to contract 1.4.0. budget_remediable is the field a caller should branch on before advising a retry: it is false for "unreadable_path" (no max_repo_files value makes a denied directory readable) and ALSO false for "unknown", because an unrecognised cause must never be answered with "raise the limit" -- guidance about whether a signal can be trusted is an allow-list, never a deny-list. TWO known asymmetries, deliberately recorded rather than papered over: (1) possibly_truncated: true can still appear with NO truncation_cause, because the per-file max_repo_files cap and the native-walk deadline set it independently of the DirectoryScanner, so "truncated implies a cause is present" is NOT an invariant a client may rely on; (2) this truncation_cause vocabulary is NOT identical to the CLI's incomplete_reason_class above, and the two must NOT be unified : MCP's truncation_cause has "unknown" where the CLI raises loudly. From contract 1.6.0 the MCP tg_search/tg_ast_search payloads ALSO carry the CLI-family incomplete_reason_class at top level, additively and only when the cause is classifiable -- both native-walk deadline paths emit "deadline", and a broad-scan refusal emits "scan_limit". An AST-backend failure sets result_incomplete and deliberately emits NO class, because a backend fault is none of the four members and the vocabulary is an allow-list. An ABSENT class therefore means "cause not classifiable", NEVER "scan complete" -- completeness is carried by result_incomplete alone. From contract 1.7.0 the same budget_remediable flag ALSO appears on the scan_limit / output_limit of every build_repo_map-backed tool -- tg_repo_map and the tg_session family -- because those handlers return the CLI payload VERBATIM. Same additive rule as above -- emitted only on a CAPPED scan, absent and byte-identical on a complete one -- and the same single allow-list (cli/incompleteness.py) supplies the value on both surfaces, because two copies is how CLI and MCP drift into opposite retry advice. From contract 1.8.0 every MCP tool JSON envelope ALSO carries a unified top-level incomplete: {status: bool, cause: str|None, budget_remediable: bool} object, injected by _inject_mcp_contract_fields (the single choke point that already stamps mcp_contract_version/schema_version on every tool response) via cli/incompleteness.py::unified_incomplete_envelope, so a client can check ONE consistent field regardless of which of the 58 tools it called instead of learning each tool's own surface-specific vocabulary (result_incomplete/truncation_cause/incomplete_reason_class/...). It is DERIVED, never a replacement: every pre-existing field above stays present and byte-identical, incomplete.status mirrors result_incomplete (default False for a tool with no incompleteness concept), incomplete.cause mirrors the free-text incomplete_reason (never the closed-vocabulary class), and incomplete.budget_remediable mirrors the tool's own budget_remediable when status is true and is forced False when it is not. A tool that builds its own incomplete key is never overwritten (setdefault). - result_incomplete alone is NOT a sufficient completeness check. It answers exactly one question -- "was the SCAN cut short?" -- and a payload can therefore report result_incomplete: false with exit 0 while still handing back materially less than it found. An agent that branches only on result_incomplete (or only on the exit code) will read those payloads as complete. Three additional fields carry that information, and their PRESENCE RULES DIFFER -- read each one's rule below rather than assuming a single convention, because "the field is absent" means different things across them: - token_budget (defs / refs / callers / impact, and the agent capsule) -- an OUTPUT cap from --max-tokens. PRESENCE RULE: emitted whenever --max-tokens is in effect, INCLUDING on a complete result, where it reads truncated: false / primary_truncated: false and carries no primary_omitted at all. So unlike the two fields below, the object's presence proves nothing on its own -- you must read primary_truncated. (The sibling omissions envelope is likewise always present, with an empty omitted_sections when nothing was trimmed.) token_budget.truncated says something was dropped for display; primary_truncated says the drop hit the PRIMARY result list, not just secondary sections; primary_omitted is how many primary rows were withheld. omissions.omitted_sections[] names each trimmed section with a reason. This is deliberately NOT a scan truncation -- the analysis ran to completion and only the rendering was capped -- which is why it stays exit 0 and does not set result_incomplete (see the OUTPUT-cap rule above). That distinction is correct and load-bearing, but it means primary_truncated is the ONLY field that will tell you the answer you are reading is a subset. Branch on it. Concretely: tg callers . <symbol> --json can return 1 of 4 callers with result_incomplete: false, not_found: false, exit 0, and token_budget.primary_omitted: 3 -- every one of those is contract-correct, and only the last one is the whole story. Raise --max-tokens (or pass --max-tokens 0) to get the full set. - incomplete_paths_count (compiled-native --json / --ndjson search envelopes) -- how many walk-error EVENTS the search hit, alongside result_incomplete and incomplete_reason_class. Omitted entirely on a complete walk. Despite the name it is NOT a count of distinct paths, and it can exceed one: the walker visits each ROOT you pass, without deduplicating overlapping roots, so tg search PAT . src walks src twice and one unreadable directory under it raises the count twice. With overlapping roots, a failed path can be visited repeatedly, so the number is a faithful count of failed reads rather than a defect -- but a caller that needs "how many distinct places could I not look" must not read this field as that answer. For a genuine per-path count see MCP's unreadable_path_count, which is a different field with different semantics (directory_scanner.py, once per failed os.scandir) and is deliberately NOT unified with this one. - not_found -- asserts the symbol is genuinely ABSENT, and is therefore only meaningful on a scan that finished. It is suppressed whenever the scan was truncated, so not_found: false on an exit-2 payload means "we did not finish looking", NOT "we found it". - output_limit (tg map, tg blast-radius, and the defs / refs / callers / impact symbol commands) -- an OUTPUT cap from --max-files/--max-callers/--max-tests. It describes DISPLAY omissions, never analysis completeness: result_incomplete describes the analysis/scan, and an output-only cap keeps it false with exit 0, disclosing instead via an OUTPUT LIMITED: display omitted N caller(s)/file(s)/test file(s)/import consumer(s); raise --max-* to see more caveat (a trailing note: in text; in --mermaid a tg_output_limited advisory node, distinct from the scan-truncation tg_incomplete node). A capped subset is NOT exhaustive: read the exact omitted_* counts and raise the named knob to get the rest. Only a SCAN truncation (scan_limit/caller_scan_limit/partial/caller_scan_truncated, or a preexisting upstream-stamped result_incomplete: true) exits 2 with a leading INCOMPLETE RESULT warning; when a scan truncation and an output cap are both present the caveat discloses both facts, and the deadline is never masked by the display cap. The general rule, and the reason this list is written out rather than left implicit: a field that a caller must read to detect incompleteness has to be NAMED in this contract, or the contract fails open -- a consumer who does not know the field exists cannot branch on it, and silence reads as completeness. Adding a new truncation or omission channel means adding it here in the same change.

  • A THIRD backend name reaches --cpu --json on a plain pip/uvx install: "RustCoreBackend". The paragraph above describes the machine that HAS the compiled native tg binary, where --cpu --json reports "NativeCpuBackend" (emitted by the Rust binary itself, rust_core/src/routing.rs). A wheel install has no such binary, so the same command is answered by the PYTHON RustCoreBackend class over the tensor_grep.rust_core extension, reporting routing_backend = "RustCoreBackend" / routing_reason = "rust_regex". This is not cosmetic, because the allow-list rule stated above is keyed on these exact strings. A consumer who allow-lists only "CPUBackend" and the rg route will correctly REJECT "RustCoreBackend" (fail-closed, which is the desired direction) -- but will do so while the scan was in fact complete, so the failure mode is a false incompleteness rather than a false completeness. Both names must therefore be in the reader's model: "NativeCpuBackend" = compiled front door, "RustCoreBackend" = Python-over-extension, and neither carries the native-envelope incompleteness fields the rg route and the Python CPUBackend route provide.

  • Two similarly-named count fields mean different things and can legitimately disagree in one payload. scan_limit.scanned_files counts files the repo-map COLLECTION stage actually walked/parsed. deadline_limit.files_scanned counts files the specific deadline-bounded stage got through before the budget expired, against deadline_limit.files_total. A single tg refs ... --deadline 0.1 --json payload can therefore carry scan_limit.scanned_files: 247 and deadline_limit.files_scanned: 0 simultaneously and be internally consistent -- the map was already built, and the reference-scan that consumes it never started. Neither field is a repo-wide total; for "was this complete?" use partial / result_incomplete / the exit code, never a comparison between these two numbers.

  • deadline_limit's scanned/total pairs name WHICH stage ran out of budget; deadline_exceeded alone cannot. deadline_exceeded is a single shared boolean, and several stages read the same clock, so a caller seeing it knows only THAT the budget expired. Each deadline-bounded stage therefore contributes its own pair, emitted additively and only when that stage actually ran: files_scanned/files_total (repo-map collection), caller_files_scanned/caller_files_total (tg callers), reference_files_scanned/reference_files_total (tg refs), importer_candidates_scanned/importer_candidates_total (reverse-import walk), source_candidates_examined/source_candidates_total (definition preference), and test_candidates_scanned/test_candidates_total (the whole-repo test-relevance scorer on the callers/impact/refs paths). A pair's ABSENCE means that stage did not run, not that it completed. test_candidates_* additionally SUMS ACROSS SCANS: tg callers reaches the test-relevance scorer twice when the symbol has callers (the second scan sits behind an if caller_files: guard; tg impact and tg refs reach it once), so a 6-test repo typically reports test_candidates_total: 12, and 6/12 there means the first scan completed and the second never started -- NOT 50% coverage of the repo's tests. Read the pair as "candidate slots walked out of slots this command was going to walk", never as a count of distinct test files. scanned may legitimately be 0 against a non-zero total — the stage was reached and stopped before its first item, which is still an honest attribution; total is stamped before the loop so this reports 0/N rather than a 0/0 that would read as "never ran". Reason a pair is missing, not a scanned of zero.

  • tg checkpoint undo --json distinguishes a MISSING checkpoint from a CORRUPT one. error: "checkpoint_not_found" means the record could not be resolved. error: "checkpoint_corrupt" (added in this change) means the record WAS found and its snapshot blobs are missing or unreadable, so undo refused before touching a single working-tree file. Both exit 1. Before this, every undo failure reported checkpoint_not_found, which sent the reader hunting a checkpoint that was sitting right there and hid the only fact that mattered -- the snapshot cannot restore the tree. Treat this as ADDITIVE: a consumer that only knows checkpoint_not_found still sees ok: false and a human-readable detail, and the new value appears exactly where the old one was wrong.

  • tg checkpoint create [PATH] --label TEXT accepts an optional trimmed label of 1-120 printable Unicode characters. The label is carried in create/list JSON and human-readable list output, and is persisted in both checkpoint metadata and index.json; omitted labels are null in new records and absent or malformed stored labels load as null without hiding the checkpoint. Labels may repeat and never select restoration: the CLI retains its checkpoint-ID and --last forms, while MCP undo requires the checkpoint ID. MCP tg_checkpoint_create and tg_checkpoint(action="create") accept the same label; supplying it to meta-tool list or undo returns error.code = "invalid_input". Printable strings are preserved literally over MCP, including "null", numeric text, quoted text and JSON-shaped arrays or objects. Non-text values passed directly to the Python handler return invalid_input; over MCP, schema-invalid types are rejected by protocol argument validation (isError) before the handler runs. Invalid text that reaches the handler returns structured invalid_input. The storage version remains v1. Older clients that rewrite the index may discard labels they do not understand.

docs.title: 5. Operational diagnostics (tg doctor --json)
docs.text: tg doctor --json is intended for operational automation and support workflows. - The doctor payload includes top-level schema_version and doctor_schema_version. Additive minor-version schema changes must bump these fields when consumer-visible shapes change. - LSP diagnostics expose both a stable array and a keyed compatibility map. lsp.providers and top-level lsp_provider_items are the provider arrays. Top-level lsp_providers and lsp.providers_by_language are keyed by language for consumers that used the older object shape. Keyed entries include health as an alias for health_status. - Existing top-level sections remain additive-only within a major version. - Individual diagnostic fields may grow as new probes are added. - Consumers should treat missing optional fields as a valid state and ignore unknown fields. - Implicit native-binary resolution must not select stale in-tree rust_core/target/*/tg(.exe) binaries. Stale in-tree candidates should be reported under skipped_native_tg_binaries with rust_binary_version_status = stale-skipped; TG_NATIVE_TG_BINARY is the explicit opt-in for using a specific standalone binary anyway. - PATH candidate probes should distinguish tensor-grep launchers from foreign tg commands owned by other software. A foreign command ahead of the managed native front door is an environment blocker for public readiness and benchmark interpretation, not permission to remove the other command automatically.

docs.title: 6. Python Library API
docs.text: Classes and functions exposed in tensor_grep.api are stable within a major version. Internal modules (prefixed with _ or deep inside tensor_grep.core, tensor_grep.cli, or backend-specific packages) are subject to change without notice.

docs.title: 7. Explicitly unstable / experimental surface
docs.text:
The items documented in docs/EXPERIMENTAL.md are not covered by the stability guarantees in this file. - Hidden commands such as tg worker - Opt-in runtime flags such as TG_RESIDENT_AST - Temporary backend override environment variables used during migration or benchmarking

These surfaces may change, move, or be removed in minor releases.

docs.title: 8. EvidenceReceipt signing (tg evidence emit --sign / tg evidence verify)
docs.text: tg evidence emit always attaches a top-level receipt_sha256 -- a keyless SHA-256 integrity/dedup/chain digest, present whether or not the receipt is signed. Passing --sign additionally attaches signing and signature blocks; passing --previous <path> attaches previous_receipt_sha256 independent of --sign. - Algorithm: Ed25519 (cryptography's Ed25519PrivateKey/Ed25519PublicKey), chosen because a downstream verifier (for example an external service) is a separate trust domain from the machine that emits receipts -- an asymmetric signature lets it verify without ever holding a key that could forge one. tg audit's HMAC-SHA256 (audit_manifest.py) remains correct for its own same-operator local tamper-evidence use case. - Canonicalization (tg-canonical-json-v1): json.dumps(receipt_without_signature_and_receipt_sha256, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True, allow_nan=False).encode("utf-8"). Only the signature and receipt_sha256 fields are excluded from the signed/hashed bytes -- the signing block itself (including its algorithm claim) is signed, so an algorithm-downgrade or public-key-swap attack invalidates both the digest and the signature. receipt_sha256 and the Ed25519 signature are computed over the identical canonical bytes. - Number formatting is CPython-specific (cross-implementation caveat): tg-canonical-json-v1 inherits CPython's json number formatting -- notably its float.__repr__ (shortest round-trip, e.g. 0.1 + 0.2 serializes as 0.30000000000000004) and its arbitrary-precision integer output. This is not RFC 8785 / JCS canonical-number formatting. A verifier written in another runtime (JavaScript / Go) MUST reproduce CPython's exact number serialization to recompute the same canonical bytes, or its digest/signature check will spuriously fail on any receipt containing a non-trivial float. Practical guidance: tg's own receipt fields are simple (small integers, short decimals like a confidence of 0.72, and strings), which round-trip identically across implementations; a downstream verifier should either match CPython number formatting exactly or treat numeric fields with care (and any caller-supplied --cost-json should avoid high-precision floats). A future tg-canonical-json-v2 could adopt JCS if a cross-language verifier needs stricter number canonicalization. - Wire shape when signed: "signing": {"algorithm": "ed25519", "key_id": "sha256:<hex of the raw 32-byte public key>", "public_key": "<base64 raw 32 bytes>", "signed_at": "<RFC3339>", "canonicalization": "tg-canonical-json-v1", "receipt_id": "<uuid4>"} plus "signature": {"value": "<base64 signature>"}. The signature block holds only the raw signature value; the signer's identity lives in the (signed) signing block. - Trust bootstrap (never trust an embedded key for authenticity): tg evidence verify always reports the signer's key fingerprint (key_id), computed from the embedded public key's own bytes -- never from a claimed label. An embedded public key only proves internal self-consistency (anyone can generate a keypair and sign with it); actual authenticity requires an out-of-band pinned key, supplied via repeatable --trusted-key <base64-public-key> or TG_EVIDENCE_TRUSTED_KEYS (comma-separated). --require-trusted fails valid closed unless the embedded key's fingerprint matches a pinned entry (hmac.compare_digest); a trusted-key check against an unsigned receipt is always invalid, mirroring audit_manifest.py's "signing key supplied but manifest unsigned" rule. - Key management: the private key defaults to ~/.tensor-grep/keys/evidence_ed25519.key (per-user home, never the per-repo .tensor-grep/ that tg audit writes to), overridable via --signing-key / TG_EVIDENCE_SIGNING_KEY. tg evidence keygen writes the private key at file mode 0600 via an atomic create-then-rename (refusing to overwrite an existing file or write through a symlink unless --force) and the public key alongside at <path>.pub (0644). tg evidence pubkey prints the public key and key_id for registration with a downstream verifier. - Fail-closed: --sign with no resolvable signing key (or an unavailable cryptography install) exits non-zero and writes no receipt -- it never falls back to emitting an unsigned receipt. Every receipt-file read is size-bounded (rejects a file over a few megabytes) before parsing/hashing: both the primary receipt (tg evidence verify <path>) and the --previous chain file (reachable from both tg evidence verify --previous and tg evidence emit --previous). - Consumer note: signatures do not expire; replay/staleness detection (via receipt_id, signed_at, and the revision.commit_sha/dirty_tree_sha256 repo binding) is the downstream verifier's responsibility, not tg's for a standalone receipt verified directly with tg evidence verify (which has no ref-comparison flag). When a receipt is embedded in a review bundle instead, section 11 below's tg review-bundle verify --against <ref> provides an in-tool, fail-closed freshness check against a caller-supplied git ref -- the CI-gate path this note used to say tg does not provide.

docs.title: 9. Ledger claims (tg ledger claim / release / list) -- advisory, code-scoped agent coordination (Slice 1)
docs.text:
tg ledger is a local, ADVISORY, code-scoped agent-to-agent coordination plane. A claim is a lightweight, TTL-expiring, best-effort record that one agent intends to touch a symbol or file -- it is never a lock on an edit. tg ledger claim always succeeds (exit 0) even when a live overlapping claim exists from another agent; overlap information is reported for the caller to act on, and tg never refuses or blocks an edit because of it. State lives at <canonical-repo-root>/.tensor-grep/ledger/claims/index.json and is created only by the first claim in a repo (default-inert: list/release never create it).

Status: EXPERIMENTAL / preview (Slice 1), unlike section 8's EvidenceReceipt above -- the CLI surface and JSON schema documented in this section may change in a minor release. tg ledger --help and each subcommand's own --help are marked EXPERIMENTAL (Slice 1) for the same reason, mirroring how tg find's docstring is prefixed EXPERIMENTAL:.

  • PATH scoping : claim/release/list all canonicalize PATH to the nearest .git ancestor -- the SAME shared claims index for one repository, regardless of which subtree of it PATH names (.git is the one unambiguous, universally-understood repo-boundary signal; falls back to PATH taken literally, unchanged, when no .git is found, so a non-git working directory is not regressed). PATH is now preserved as the claim's scope (root-relative, POSIX-normalized -- Windows separators, a leading ./, and a trailing / are all normalized for free) instead of being (mis)used as the physical storage location. This canonicalization applies on the SAME terms to Slice 2 (record/find, below) as well -- both slices share the one _ledger_physical_root derivation (derive the current call-site membership from grep -n "_ledger_physical_root(path)" src/tensor_grep/cli/ledger_store.py, never from an enumerated list -- a name list goes stale the moment a new entry point is added); the non-git literal-PATH fallback described above is likewise shared by both slices, unchanged. Migration honesty: a claim written by a PRE-fix version through a subtree PATH lives in that subtree's old physical store (<subtree>/.tensor-grep/ledger/), which post-fix commands never read or write again -- it becomes invisible to list and unreleasable by release (no crash; the orphaned index simply sits as a dead file whose claims are TTL-expired within their own TTL window, default 15 minutes). During that window, a release targeting such a pre-fix claim reports unmatched_reason and a live_claims_elsewhere drawn from the NEW canonical store -- it cannot see the orphan -- so a just-upgraded agent should simply let the old claim expire rather than chase the release. Do not delete the whole .tensor-grep/ directory to remove an old ledger store: it may also contain sessions and durable checkpoints.
  • Exit-code contract (two states only, not the three-state symbol-command contract in section 3 above): 0 = the command completed and its JSON/text output can be trusted, including a claim with non-empty overlaps, a release that matched zero claims, and a list with zero live claims -- none of those are errors. 2 = a fail-closed condition fired and nothing was written: a claims-index lock-acquire timeout, a symlink at the index destination, a --files entry that resolves outside the repo root (../..., an absolute path, or a symlink escape), a corrupt or oversized on-disk index, or missing required arguments (claim with neither --symbol nor --files; release with neither --claim-id nor --symbol). There is no exit 1 for this command family.
  • Claim record shape: {ledger_schema_version, kind: "claim", claim_id, agent_id, symbols, files, scope, intent, note, created_at, expires_at, ttl_seconds, revision}. claim_id is claim-<UTC-compact-timestamp>-<8-hex>. scope is PATH normalized against the canonicalized repo root -- "." for the repo root itself, e.g. "core/hooks" for a subtree (see "PATH scoping" above; an entry read back from a pre-fix on-disk record with no scope key at all is stamped "." on the way out, never dropped). revision is the same {status, commit_sha, branch, dirty, dirty_tree_sha256, dirty_file_count} / {status: "unavailable", reason} shape section 8's EvidenceReceipt uses (_repo_revision_identity) -- captured for free at claim time so a caller can tell whether an overlapping claim was filed against the same commit.
  • tg ledger claim PATH [--symbol S ...] [--files a,b] [--intent edit] [--ttl SECONDS] [--agent-id ID] [--note TEXT] [--json]: --symbol is repeatable; --files is one comma-separated value of root-relative paths (traversal-refused, per the exit-2 contract above, against the canonicalized repo root). Requires at least one --symbol or --files entry.
