Response JSON: {version, schema_version, routing_backend: "Ledger", routing_reason: "ledger-claim", sidecar_used: false, ledger_schema_version, advisory: true, claim: {...}, overlaps: [...]}. overlaps lists LIVE (non-expired) claims whose symbols/files literally intersect the new claim, and is never scope-filtered (a symbol/file overlap matters regardless of which subtree each claimant used). Self-suppression -- dropping the caller's OWN other claims, since an agent overlapping itself is not a coordination conflict -- applies ONLY when the caller has a real identity. The default agent_id is the literal sentinel "anonymous", which is the ABSENCE of an identity rather than one, so two zero-config agents both filed as "anonymous" DO see each other's overlaps (ledger_store._find_overlaps gates its suppression on agent_id != _DEFAULT_AGENT_ID; pinned by tests/unit/test_anonymous_claims_are_not_one_agent.py). Each overlap entry is {claim_id, agent_id, symbols, files, intent, expires_at, revision_matches}; revision_matches is true/false only when both sides have a resolved git identity, and null (never fabricated) when either side's revision capture came back unavailable.
  • tg ledger release PATH (--claim-id ID | --symbol S) [--agent-id ID] [--json]: --claim-id releases an exact claim regardless of which agent owns it (the opaque id itself is the authorization -- e.g. an orchestrator garbage-collecting a crashed sub-agent's claim). --symbol releases only the resolved --agent-id's OWN live claim(s) covering that symbol, so a common/guessable symbol name can never release another agent's claim by accident. PATH only resolves WHICH repository's canonical claims index this call operates on (see "PATH scoping" above) -- it does NOT filter which claim matches (deliberately unchanged from the pre-fix contract, unlike list below: adding scope-rollup matching to release could let a call silently drop an unrelated sibling agent's claim just because it shares a symbol name under a broader/ancestor scope). Response JSON: {..., routing_reason: "ledger-release", released: [...], released_count, listed_scope, unmatched_reason, live_claims_elsewhere: [...], live_claims_elsewhere_count, live_claims_elsewhere_truncated}. Releasing zero matching claims (already released, already expired, or never existed) is not an error and does not change the exit code -- but unmatched_reason (a short, human-readable string) and live_claims_elsewhere (bounded to 10 entries, each {claim_id, agent_id, scope, symbols, files, intent, expires_at}, with live_claims_elsewhere_count as the true total and live_claims_elsewhere_truncated set when the count exceeds what is shown) are now populated so a wrong --claim-id/--symbol is self-diagnosing instead of an indistinguishable bare released_count: 0. listed_scope is PATH normalized the same way a claim's scope is. All five of these fields are None/empty/0/false (as appropriate) when released_count > 0.
  • tg ledger list PATH [--symbol S] [--agent-id ID] [--json]: pure read -- prunes expired entries for display only and never writes (so list alone can never create .tensor-grep/ledger/). Rolls scope UP: listing a broader/ancestor PATH (e.g. the default ., the repo root) shows every live claim scoped to it OR to any descendant subtree -- e.g. a claim made with tg ledger claim core/hooks shows up in tg ledger list (default .) and in tg ledger list core, but not in tg ledger list docs (a disjoint sibling) and not the other way around (tg ledger list core/hooks/sub does NOT show a claim scoped to core or to . -- rollup is one-directional: a narrower listing never gains visibility into a broader ancestor scope). Containment is segment-wise (lexical), never a raw string-prefix test -- a claim scoped to core/ho does not falsely match a listing of core/hoodie or vice versa. --symbol/--agent-id filters apply AFTER the scope-rollup filter, combined as AND. Response JSON: {..., routing_reason: "ledger-list", claims: [...], count} -- each entry in claims carries its own scope.
  • agent_id resolution: --agent-id (when non-blank) wins; else TG_LEDGER_AGENT_ID; else TG_EVIDENCE_AGENT_ID (shared fallback with tg evidence); else the literal string "anonymous". Recorded verbatim, never inferred from process/user identity. Do not put secrets in --agent-id or --note -- both are written to a plaintext, per-repo, multi-agent-readable JSON file with no access control beyond the filesystem.
  • TTL and expiry: default 900 seconds, overridable per-claim with --ttl or globally via TG_LEDGER_CLAIM_TTL_SECONDS. A dead agent's claim needs no special crash handling -- it simply stops appearing in list/overlap results once expires_at passes; physical removal from disk happens lazily on the next claim/release write (a pure list never rewrites the index). A record with a missing or unparseable expires_at (corrupt write, foreign edit) is treated as already-expired, not as immortal.
  • Concurrency and DoS bounds: every write (claim/release) is a read-modify-write serialized under the same per-root index_lock primitive tg session/tg checkpoint use (cross-process safe, self-healing stale-lock reclaim, no lost inserts under concurrent writers) -- "per-root" now means per CANONICALIZED root, so two tg ledger claim calls for two different subtrees of the SAME repository correctly serialize against each other, while two calls against two genuinely different (non-git, or differently-.git-rooted) directories still do not. The on-disk index is capped at 256 live claims per root (oldest created_at evicted first) as a bound distinct from TTL expiry -- a flood of claims with a long TTL cannot grow the index without limit even though none of them are individually expired yet. The index read is byte-bounded before parsing (8 MiB) as a pre-parse DoS guard.
  • Not yet built (future slices, do not assume present): no MCP tool surface (CLI-only in Slice 1), no task-level or cross-repo coordination, no automatic claim renewal/heartbeat, no enforcement mechanism of any kind -- tg ledger reports; it never blocks, queues, or serializes an actual edit.

docs.title: 10. Ledger findings (tg ledger record / find) -- content-addressed reuse of computed artifacts (Slice 2)
docs.text:
tg ledger record/find extend the Slice 1 coordination plane (section 9) with a content-addressed artifact-reuse cache: one agent records an evidence-receipt/blast-radius/context-pack/repo-map artifact it already computed; a sibling agent finds it by symbol and reuses the artifact instead of recomputing -- the artifact reuse mechanism. State lives at <root>/.tensor-grep/ledger/findings/index.json (a separate index from claims' claims/index.json) plus <root>/.tensor-grep/ledger/findings/blobs/<receipt_sha256>.json (one file per DISTINCT artifact, content-addressed and dedup'd -- recording the identical artifact twice writes the same blob path). Created only by the first record in a repo (default-inert: find never creates it, mirroring claims' list). record/find canonicalize PATH to the nearest .git ancestor on the SAME terms as Slice 1 -- see the PATH-scoping bullet in section 9 for the derivation (_ledger_physical_root, membership derived from its call sites, not enumerated); a record/find from a different subtree of the same repository shares the repo-root index, not a separate one.

Status: EXPERIMENTAL / preview (Slice 2), same posture as section 9 -- CLI surface and JSON schema may change in a minor release. tg ledger record --help / tg ledger find --help are marked EXPERIMENTAL (Slice 2). Default-OFF in the sense that matters: nothing in tg agent/tg edit-plan consults the ledger automatically in this slice -- record/find are explicit-invoke only (automatic consultation is not implemented).

  • PATH scoping — record/find canonicalize on the SAME terms as Slice 1. Both resolve PATH to the nearest .git ancestor via _ledger_physical_root (grep -n "_ledger_physical_root" src/tensor_grep/cli/ledger_store.py for the current call-site membership -- do not enumerate or count the sites here, that list rots the moment a new entry point is added), so tg ledger find ./src sees an artifact recorded at the repo root. Slice 2 was genuinely more path-literal than Slice 1 once; section 9's scoping bullet and this one are now both current. Re-derive the membership from the call sites above rather than trusting either prose bullet by itself: a behaviour that spreads to a new call site does not retroactively update a sentence that enumerated the old ones -- that is what happened here once already.
  • Exit-code contract for record (two states, same shape as section 9's claim/release/list): 0 = the artifact was ingested (or an identical artifact was already present -- dedup is not an error) and nothing else is asserted. 2 = a fail-closed condition fired and nothing was written: missing --receipt, an --artifact-kind outside {blast-radius, evidence-receipt, context-pack, repo-map}, a missing/oversized (>8 MiB)/non-JSON --receipt file, a findings-index lock-acquire timeout, or a write failure.
  • Exit-code contract for find (three states -- distinct from every other tg ledger subcommand, deliberately mirroring the tg defs/callers/blast-radius symbol-command contract in section 3): 0 = at least one returned finding is fresh: true (safe to reuse). 1 = zero returned findings are fresh (recompute) -- this covers both "no finding matched --symbol/--artifact-kind at all" and "matches exist but none are fresh," including when --fresh-only filtered every match away. 2 = a fail-closed condition fired: missing/blank --symbol, a corrupt/oversized findings index, or -- the case unique to find -- a blob that fails its integrity check (see below). A harness branches on this directly: if tg ledger find PATH --symbol S --fresh-only; then reuse the artifact; else compute; fi.
  • Finding record shape: {ledger_schema_version, kind: "finding", finding_id, agent_id, artifact_kind, symbol, receipt_sha256, blob_relpath, signed, key_id, revision, created_at, expires_at, ttl_seconds}. finding_id is finding-<UTC-compact-timestamp>-<8-hex>. receipt_sha256 is tensor_grep.cli.evidence_signing.receipt_digest() computed over the artifact JSON -- the SAME canonical-JSON content-address function tg evidence uses (tg-canonical-json-v1: compact, key-sorted, ASCII-only, signature/receipt_sha256 fields excluded), so a plain (non-receipt) artifact hashes identically regardless of incidental whitespace, and an artifact that already happens to carry its own receipt_sha256/signature fields (a real EvidenceReceipt) is not self-referentially corrupted by them. revision is the same _repo_revision_identity shape sections 8/9 use. signed/key_id are captured at record time from the artifact's own (self-claimed, unverified) signing block presence -- never proof of authenticity by themselves (see the trust-bootstrap rule below).
  • tg ledger record PATH --receipt FILE.json [--artifact-kind K] [--symbol S] [--agent-id ID] [--ttl SECONDS] [--json]: --artifact-kind defaults to evidence-receipt and is validated against the fixed enum at WRITE time (rejects garbage before it enters the store). --receipt is read bounded (refuses over 8 MiB before parsing -- the same "pre-auth unbounded read" DoS guard section 8/9 use elsewhere) and must parse as a JSON object. Response JSON: {version, schema_version, routing_backend: "Ledger", routing_reason: "ledger-record", sidecar_used: false, ledger_schema_version, advisory: true, finding: {...}}.
  • tg ledger find PATH --symbol S [--artifact-kind K] [--fresh-only] [--trusted-key KEY ...] [--json]: --symbol is required (validated in the store, not by Typer, so a missing value still returns the standard {"error": {...}} JSON envelope under --json rather than a bare Click usage error). --artifact-kind, UNLIKE record, is a plain string-equality filter at READ time -- not validated against the enum, so an unrecognized value simply matches nothing rather than erroring. Response JSON: {..., routing_reason: "ledger-find", findings: [...], count, any_fresh}; each entry in findings is the finding record plus fresh: bool and key_trusted: bool | None (null when the finding is unsigned or no --trusted-key/TG_EVIDENCE_TRUSTED_KEYS was supplied).
  • Freshness (revision-primary, never silently served as current): a finding is fresh: true only when BOTH its captured revision and the CURRENT repo's _repo_revision_identity(root) resolved to status: "present" AND their commit_sha AND dirty_tree_sha256 both match exactly -- so a single uncommitted edit anywhere in the tracked/untracked diff (which changes dirty_tree_sha256) flips a finding to fresh: false even on the same commit. An unresolvable revision on EITHER side (not a git repo, git unavailable) fails closed to fresh: false, never fabricated. Both capture (at record time) and the current-state recheck (at find time) exclude the ledger's own .tensor-grep/ledger/ subtree from the dirty-tree computation (_repo_revision_identity(..., exclude_prefixes=(".tensor-grep/ledger",)), mirroring section 8's tg codemap --check self-dirty fix) -- otherwise the very act of recording would make the repo read as dirty against itself and poison every subsequent freshness check. This is a wall-clock-independent check computed fresh on every find call; the TTL below is a separate, secondary backstop.
  • Integrity (fail-closed, never serve tampered data): every finding actually being returned (i.e. surviving the --symbol/--artifact-kind/--fresh-only filters) has its blob read back and its content digest recomputed via receipt_digest; a mismatch (or a missing/oversized/non-JSON blob) raises and the WHOLE find call exits 2 -- it never silently drops the bad finding and returns the rest, and never serves unverified content. A finding excluded by --fresh-only is never integrity-checked (only findings about to be served are). --trusted-key/TG_EVIDENCE_TRUSTED_KEYS additionally re-verifies a signed finding's embedded signature against the CALLER's current trust config (which may differ from whatever was configured at record time) to compute key_trusted; this mirrors section 8's trust-bootstrap rule exactly -- an embedded public key alone proves internal consistency, never authenticity.
  • TTL, cap, and GC: a wall-clock backstop TTL defaults to 86400 seconds (24h; overridable per-record with --ttl or globally via TG_LEDGER_FINDING_TTL_SECONDS) -- deliberately far longer-lived than a claim's 900s default, since a finding is a reusable artifact pointer, not a short-lived coordination signal. The index is capped at 512 live findings per root; total on-disk bytes across all DISTINCT (dedup'd) blobs is separately capped (default 256 MiB, TG_LEDGER_MAX_BLOB_BYTES) since a flood of small findings could stay under the count cap while a few large artifacts still grow disk unboundedly. Either cap evicts the oldest created_at findings first. Every record call prunes TTL-expired findings and garbage-collects any blob no longer referenced by a live finding (a shared/dedup'd blob is kept until its LAST referencing finding is gone).
  • Not yet built (future slices, do not assume present): no automatic tg agent/edit-plan consultation (explicit-invoke only in Slice 2), no MCP tool surface, no manual release/delete for a findings entry (rely on TTL/cap eviction), no cross-repo lookup.

docs.title: 11. Review bundles (tg review-bundle create / verify) -- evidence-receipt CI gate
docs.text:
tg review-bundle create packages an audit manifest plus optional scan results, checkpoint metadata, a manifest diff, and (additive) signed EvidenceReceipts into one JSON artifact; tg review-bundle verify re-checks its integrity, signatures, and -- when asked -- receipt trust and freshness against a git ref. This section documents the additive --receipt / --against / --trusted-key / --require-trusted surface that closes the loop between section 8's EvidenceReceipt signing and an actual CI gate.

  • evidence_receipts component (optional, additive): _REVIEW_BUNDLE_COMPONENTS now includes evidence_receipts alongside audit_manifest (required), scan_results, checkpoint_metadata, and diff (all optional). A bundle created without --receipt sets evidence_receipts: null, exactly like the other optional components when their source flag is omitted; a bundle written by a pre-this-feature tg (no evidence_receipts key at all) verifies identically, since the generic per-component checksum loop treats "key absent" and "key present with null" the same way for a non-required component. Adding this component to the existing checksum/bundle_sha256 machinery is sufficient for it to inherit the SAME tamper-evidence every other component already has -- no separate integrity mechanism was added.
  • tg review-bundle create --receipt FILE.json [--receipt FILE2.json ...]: repeatable. Each path is read through evidence_signing.read_receipt_file (the SAME bounded reader -- 5 MB pre-parse DoS guard, JSON-object validation -- tg evidence verify uses; not reimplemented). The parsed receipt objects are embedded verbatim, in argument order, as evidence_receipts. The text-mode summary line's components= list additively includes evidence_receipts when at least one --receipt was supplied; --json output's top-level evidence_receipts key is null when omitted, matching scan_results/checkpoint_metadata/diff.
  • tg review-bundle verify BUNDLE --against REF [--trusted-key KEY ...] [--require-trusted]: for each embedded receipt, re-verifies its digest/signature/trust via evidence_signing.verify_receipt (the identical function tg evidence verify calls -- no separate crypto path) and, only when --against is supplied, its freshness against REF. --trusted-key (repeatable, base64 Ed25519 public key from tg evidence pubkey) and TG_EVIDENCE_TRUSTED_KEYS (comma-separated fallback) behave exactly like section 8's tg evidence verify flags of the same name, including the same stderr warning when a trusted key is supplied without --require-trusted (an untrusted embedded key then still reports valid=true for that receipt's signature check). Response JSON additively carries receipts (a list, one entry per embedded receipt, {index, receipt_sha256, signature: {...same shape tg evidence verify returns...}, freshness: {...only when --against was given...}, valid}) and, only when --against was supplied, top-level against: {ref, resolved_commit_sha, valid, error}. Every receipt's valid and (when applicable) against.valid are ANDed into the bundle's existing top-level valid; because review-bundle verify --json already exits 1 whenever valid is false (section-3-style H1 contract, pre-existing), an unsigned/untrusted/tampered/stale/unresolvable-ref receipt fails the whole command with no new exit-code logic.
  • Ref resolution is fail-closed, never bundle-path-derived: --against REF is resolved via git rev-parse --verify REF^{commit} run against the verifying process's OWN current working directory (e.g. the CI job's checkout) -- never a path embedded in the (attacker-influenceable) bundle JSON, which would let a tampered bundle redirect ref resolution. An unresolvable ref (typo, ref not fetched, not a git repository, git missing or timing out) sets against.valid = false with a populated against.error and fails the WHOLE bundle closed (valid = false) even when the bundle carries zero receipts -- there is no "the ref didn't resolve, so skip this check" outcome.
  • Freshness definition (commit + clean tree, not the CI working tree's own dirty-tree hash): a receipt is fresh against a resolved --against commit only when its revision.status == "present", revision.commit_sha equals the resolved commit, AND revision.dirty is false. This deliberately does NOT re-derive and compare a dirty_tree_sha256 against the CI checkout's live working tree the way section 10's ledger-finding freshness check does -- a CI checkout can legitimately be sitting on a merge commit (or an actions/checkout ref) whose tree differs from the PR-head tree the receipt was captured against, so comparing tree hashes here would falsely flag every receipt stale. A receipt captured against a dirty working tree fails regardless of commit match, since a dirty capture is not reproducible from a commit alone.
  • CRITICAL CI wiring trap -- use the PR head SHA, never $GITHUB_SHA: in a GitHub Actions pull_request workflow, $GITHUB_SHA (and the default actions/checkout ref) resolves to an ephemeral merge commit of the PR branch into the base branch, not the PR's actual head commit. Passing --against "$GITHUB_SHA" (or omitting an explicit ref: on actions/checkout) means every embedded receipt's revision.commit_sha -- captured against the real PR head -- will NEVER match, and the gate fails RED on every single PR regardless of whether the evidence is actually fresh. The correct value is the pull_request event's head SHA (github.event.pull_request.head.sha), paired with an explicit actions/checkout ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} so the checkout the receipt was captured against and the ref verified against are the same commit. See docs/enterprise_review_bundle_ci.md for a full worked CI recipe.
  • CRITICAL presence caveat -- integrity alone does NOT prove evidence is present: a bundle with evidence_receipts null, absent, or [] verifies valid = true by default (an empty/missing OPTIONAL component is valid, exactly like scan_results/checkpoint_metadata/diff). Because the keyless checksums and bundle_sha256 are plain SHA-256 (no signing key required to recompute them), an author with write access to review-bundle.json can strip every embedded receipt, recompute those checksums to stay internally consistent, and the bundle will still verify green with no evidence at all -- integrity alone only proves "this JSON file is internally self-consistent," not "genuine evidence is present." --min-receipts and --expect-key below are the opt-in policy levers that close this: only read a passing tg review-bundle verify as proof genuine evidence is present when the gate was run with --min-receipts >= 1 (and --expect-key when a specific signer must be represented).
  • tg review-bundle verify BUNDLE --min-receipts N (default 0 = no enforcement, back-compat): after the existing checks above are computed, if the count of embedded receipts that are present, well-formed, AND pass signature/trust/freshness verification (i.e. each has receipts[].valid = true under whatever --require-trusted/--against were also passed) is less than N, verification fails closed (valid = false) with a reason string "policy requires >=N valid evidence receipts; found M". N = 0 (the default) is always trivially satisfied and adds no new top-level field -- byte-identical output to before this flag existed.
  • tg review-bundle verify BUNDLE --expect-key KEY_ID (repeatable, default none): requires that at least one valid, embedded receipt was signed by each named key_id (the SAME sha256:<hex> fingerprint format tg evidence pubkey and receipts[].signature.key_id already use -- reused, not reinvented). A named key with no matching valid receipt fails verification closed with a reason string naming the missing key_id. This pins WHICH signer(s) are REQUIRED to be represented, distinct from --trusted-key (section 8), which pins which signers are cryptographically TRUSTED at all -- an org might trust several keys (--trusted-key) while requiring evidence specifically from one of them (--expect-key).
  • policy JSON field (additive, only present when --min-receipts > 0 or --expect-key is used): {min_receipts, valid_receipt_count, min_receipts_satisfied, expect_key_ids, missing_expect_key_ids, expect_keys_satisfied, valid, reasons}. policy.valid is ANDed into the bundle's top-level valid exactly like every other check family in this section; omitting both flags omits this field entirely (not merely a null/trivial value), so a caller that never opts in sees byte-identical JSON to before this hardening.
  • What this does NOT change: tg review-bundle create/verify without --receipt/--against/--min-receipts/--expect-key are byte-for-byte the same contract as before this section -- no required component changed, no exit-code semantics changed, no existing field was renamed or removed. tg evidence emit/verify (section 8) are unchanged; --against/--min-receipts/--expect-key are review-bundle-only surfaces, not new tg evidence verify flags.

docs.title: Contributor onboarding
docs.text:
Start with the getting-started guide to try tensor-grep on a small project. Read the architecture guide to understand native routing, Python orchestration, repository context, sessions, and MCP.

For development setup and validation, follow CONTRIBUTING.md. AGENTS.md records the public contribution requirements for humans and coding assistants, including command registration, compatibility, security review, and release checks.

docs.title: Find the right reference
docs.text: Task Reference Install and check platform support Installation, support matrix Understand routing and failure behavior Routing policy, contracts Use CLI or MCP from another tool API reference, automation recipes Validate a performance change Benchmarks, tool comparison Understand CI or prepare a release CI pipeline, release checklist Choose a public contributor skill Skill index

docs.title: Public and private material
docs.text: The repository includes a small, reviewed set of product and contributor skills. Internal operating procedures, unpublished research, local configuration, and private workflows belong in a private skill store. See the publication policy.

docs.title: Experimental features
docs.text: As of 2026-10-06, this page describes optional features with narrower support or compatibility limits than core text search. They may need extra dependencies, project setup, or a specific build. Do not assume they are enabled by a basic install.

docs.title: tg find: experimental result search
docs.text:
tg find combines text retrieval with ranking options for finding potentially relevant files or passages. The command remains experimental, including when it uses BM25 ranking. BM25 is a local ranking method that orders text results by how well their words match the query; it is not a generative model and does not establish that a result is correct.

Some tg find modes can use dense embeddings. A dense embedding is a numerical representation of text used to find passages with similar meaning, including when they do not share exact words. Dense mode is optional; without its dependencies, tg find reports that it is using BM25 only. To try dense matching, explicitly run:

tg install-dense

This installs the semantic Python extra and fetches a checksum-pinned model of about 65 MB. The dense path uses CPU and NumPy; it does not require Torch or a GPU. The command needs network access, and nothing downloads automatically when you run tg find. For GPU-specific requirements, see the GPU runbook.

Treat ranked results as suggestions to inspect. The ranking may vary with the chosen backend, model, and corpus. rg remains a useful baseline for exact text search, and tg search has a separate, documented search contract.

docs.title: GPU execution and calibration
docs.text:
GPU support is opt-in and experimental. A CPU-only installation does not need GPU libraries. GPU execution requires a compatible build, device, drivers, and supported route. A GPU-related package or CI matrix entry by itself does not show that a request ran on the GPU. Inspect route evidence described in GPU troubleshooting when validating a specific request.

tg calibrate measures the CPU/GPU crossover for a supported GPU build. It helps the router decide which workload sizes may justify GPU execution. It does not create, rebuild, or warm .tg_index, and CPU-only builds cannot perform GPU calibration. See routing policy for index and backend selection.

The optional BM25-only behavior can run locally without an API key or GPU. Dense dependencies and GPU components are separate opt-ins; do not install them just to follow the first-search guide.

docs.title: Resident AST worker
docs.text:
The hidden tg worker command can keep AST project data available in a resident process for specialized repeated workflows. It is enabled with TG_RESIDENT_AST=1 and is not started by core search. The workflow is experimental, uses local interprocess communication, and may change or be removed in a minor release. It is not a general recommendation for accelerating every scan.

See the resident worker runbook for its operational details. Review contracts before relying on it in a production workflow.

docs.title: Support boundary
docs.text: These features are outside the stable compatibility guarantees. They may fall back, refuse a request, or require a different dependency set from core text search. Keep a tested text-search path available, inspect structured route and completeness fields where offered, and check the support matrix before selecting a deployment target.

docs.title: Runtime switches for testing and diagnosis
docs.text:
These environment variables change routing behavior and are intended for testing or diagnosis. Leave them unset for ordinary use unless you are following a specific troubleshooting procedure:

  • TG_FORCE_CPU=1 requests CPU routing for search commands; it does not enable GPU execution.
  • TG_RUST_EARLY_POSITIONAL_RG=1 enables an early rg passthrough attempt for eligible bare positional searches. It has an effect only when rg is available and the invocation fits the supported passthrough surface.
  • TG_RESIDENT_AST=1 enables the experimental resident AST worker workflow described above; it does not start a worker by itself.

docs.title: Hotfix & Rollback Procedure
docs.text: This document outlines the operational procedures for addressing critical bugs or security vulnerabilities in tensor-grep production releases.

docs.title: 1. Hotfix Release Procedure
docs.text:
When a critical issue requires an immediate patch, the preferred path is still a corrective patch release through the normal main + semantic-release flow. Do not manually create release tags while semantic-release is authoritative.

  1. Branching and scope freeze: Create a short-lived hotfix branch from the current main after rebasing to origin. 

    git checkout main
git pull --rebase origin main
git checkout -b hotfix/<issue>-vX.Y.Z
    Keep the patch minimal. Do not batch unrelated cleanup or feature work into the hotfix.

  2. Patching: Cherry-pick the specific bugfix commits or implement the minimal required correction directly on the hotfix branch.

  3. Validation: Run the local quality gates and any relevant benchmark before the fix is proposed for merge. 

    uv run ruff check .
uv run mypy src/tensor_grep
uv run pytest -q
    For hot-path behavior changes, also run the relevant benchmark from benchmarks/ and compare against the accepted baseline.

  4. Release through main: Open a PR with a conventional patch title such as fix: correct <hotfix subject>.

  5. Merge with Squash and merge so the validated PR title becomes the commit subject on main.
  6. Let semantic-release generate vX.Y.(Z+1) and publish the corrected artifacts.
  7. Confirm CI, parity checks, SBOM generation, provenance, and release asset validation are green on the exact merged commit.

docs.title: 2. Rollback Procedure
docs.text: If a deployed version causes severe regressions, select a previously verified version from an available install channel. The registry-specific commands below apply only after that channel has been published; see installation.

docs.title: Winget (Windows, after registry publication)
docs.text: winget install oimiragieo.tensor-grep --version A.B.C

docs.title: pip (Python)
docs.text: pip install tensor-grep==A.B.C

docs.title: Homebrew (macOS, after tap publication)
docs.text: Homebrew users should use the exact URL to the previous formula commit or download the binary directly from the GitHub Releases page.

docs.title: 3. Reproducible Release Verification
docs.text: To verify that a published binary matches the source code: 1. Clone the repository and checkout the exact tag (for example vX.Y.Z). 2. Execute the build scripts in scripts/build_binaries.py using the exact Rust/Python toolchains specified in .github/workflows/release.yml. 3. Compare the SHA256 hashes of the generated binaries against the CHECKSUMS.txt provided in the GitHub Release assets.

docs.title: Local CI harness
docs.text: scripts/ci-local/ runs selected Linux Rust and Python checks in a CPU-capped Docker container. It is a development pre-check, not a replacement for the hosted workflow or proof that another operating system passes.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
From the repository root:

scripts/ci-local/run.sh
scripts/ci-local/run.sh rust
scripts/ci-local/run.sh python
TG_CI_CPUS=2 scripts/ci-local/run.sh
scripts/ci-local/run.sh shell

The default CPU cap is 4. Select a cap appropriate to the host and other workloads. CPU limits do not bound memory, disk I/O, or Docker VM overhead. The shell lane is for debugging and reports no test verdict. Named Cargo volumes support cache reuse across runs.

docs.title: Coverage boundary
docs.text:
A local pass covers only commands that actually ran. Read the harness's THIS RUN DID NOT EXECUTE banner and compare the command list with .github/workflows/ci.yml. Windows, macOS, other Python versions, release jobs, and separate lint, audit, readiness, and benchmark gates require their own checks.

tests/unit/test_ci_local_harness_parity.py pins mirrored workflow values such as Cargo and pytest invocations, dependency setup, and symlink-test configuration. These checks detect selected configuration drift; matching strings do not prove that the container reproduces a hosted runner's environment.

docs.title: Container pitfalls
docs.text:
• Run permission tests as the intended non-root user. Root can bypass the refusal that a test is intended to exercise.
  • Check volume ownership after an image or user change. Preserve useful cached data before recreating a volume.
  • Confirm executable mappings are allowed where the environment and extensions are installed; noexec can prevent collection from reaching a test.
  • Compare environment variables with the hosted job. An extra override can change fail-closed routing and make a local result misleading.
  • Install tools for the lane that needs them. A cached native binary or extra sg installation can cause tests to run that a different environment skips.
  • On Git Bash/MSYS, path conversion can rewrite arguments passed to native executables. Apply MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 only where needed for container mounts.
  • Confirm an image rebuild succeeded before interpreting an old :latest image as the new configuration.

To debug workflow scheduling and job conditions, a workflow runner such as act may be useful, but its container image and platform coverage also differ from GitHub-hosted virtual machines. Record the actual runner and tool versions with every result; only the exact hosted run proves the hosted gate.

docs.title: Release Checklist
docs.text:
This checklist reflects the current enterprise release pipeline:

  • CI on main runs formatting/linting, Python + Rust matrices, GPU hooks, benchmark regression, release/package-manager readiness checks.
  • Semantic Release on green main creates the version/tag/release commit.
  • PyPI publish is OIDC-based and runs only when the computed release version is not already on PyPI.
  • Release asset/version consistency is enforced by scripts/validate_release_assets.py.

docs.title: 0. Enterprise-ready evidence
docs.text:
Before calling a release enterprise-ready, confirm the exact release commit has:

  • green CI on the same commit that semantic-release tagged
  • installer-critical GitHub release assets and CHECKSUMS.txt present on the GitHub release
  • SBOMs, provenance, and signing metadata present when the release path produces them
  • package-manager bundle validation complete
  • public docs aligned:
  • docs/SUPPORT_MATRIX.md
  • docs/CONTRACTS.md
  • docs/HOTFIX_PROCEDURE.md
  • docs/EXPERIMENTAL.md
  • operator runbooks aligned with the shipped behavior

docs.title: 1. Pre-merge requirements
docs.text:
1. Sync local branch: 
    git checkout main
git pull --rebase origin main
  2. Confirm version-bearing files are aligned:
  3. pyproject.toml
  4. rust_core/Cargo.toml
  5. npm/package.json
  6. scripts/tensor-grep.rb
  7. scripts/oimiragieo.tensor-grep.yaml
  8. Run local release consistency guard: 
    uv run python scripts/validate_release_assets.py
  9. Run local quality gates: 
    uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check --preview .
uv run mypy src/tensor_grep
uv run pytest tests -v --tb=short
  10. Set the PR title to the intended semantic-release bump so squash merge can drive versioning:
  11. feat: ... -> minor
  12. fix: ... or perf: ... -> patch
  13. feat!: ... / fix!: ... -> major
  14. docs: ..., test: ..., chore: ..., ci: ..., build: ... -> no release
  15. Merge release-bearing PRs with Squash and merge so the validated PR title becomes the commit subject on main.

docs.title: 2. CI gate requirements on main
docs.text:
1. Push to main only after local checks pass.
  2. Ensure all required jobs are green:
  3. release-intent on pull requests
  4. Formatting & Linting
  5. release-readiness
  6. package-manager-readiness
  7. test-python matrix
  8. test-rust-core matrix
  9. test-gpu-nvidia
  10. benchmark-regression
  11. Confirm no benchmark regression gate failure.

docs.title: 3. Release and publication flow
docs.text:
1. Do not manually bump tags when semantic-release is active.
  2. A branch push or open PR starts PR CI only. It is not a release, not a released version, and not complete release state.
  3. Release versioning starts only after a release-bearing PR is squash-merged to main, because semantic-release reads the final main commit subject.
  4. Let the Semantic Release job infer the next version from the squash-merge commit title created from the PR title.
  5. Let the Semantic Release job create:
  6. release commit
  7. Git tag vX.Y.Z
  8. GitHub release metadata Main CI then uploads installer-critical GitHub release assets to that tag before publish-pypi is allowed to run.
  9. Fetch the release commit before local final verification: 
    git fetch origin main --tags
git pull --ff-only origin main
    This matters because local main can otherwise remain on the pre-release fix commit while origin/main has already advanced to chore(release): vX.Y.Z [skip ci].
  10. If semantic-release reports released=true, confirm downstream jobs pass:
  11. build-release-native-assets
  12. publish-github-release-assets
  13. release-native macOS amd64 asset is built on macos-15-intel, not macos-latest
  14. If publish_pypi=true, confirm PyPI jobs pass:
  15. build-pypi-wheels
  16. build-pypi-sdist
  17. validate-pypi-artifacts
  18. publish-pypi
  19. publish-success-gate
  20. parity gate step Verify release version parity across tag/assets/PyPI
  21. Confirm registry visibility with API evidence, not only local pip cache: 
    python - << 'PY'
import json, urllib.request
data = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen("https://pypi.org/pypi/tensor-grep/json"))
print(data["info"]["version"])
PY
    python -m pip index versions tensor-grep can lag because of client/cache behavior.
  22. If the installer or update path changed, PyPI/public installer availability is verified before release completion is reported.
  23. On main CI, confirm GitHub release asset verification passes before accepting the release:
  24. publish-github-release-assets
  25. step Verify GitHub release native asset coverage
  26. publish-success-gate step Verify GitHub release native assets for semantic-release version
  27. includes release-native CPU front doors (tg-linux-amd64-cpu, tg-macos-amd64-cpu, tg-windows-amd64-cpu.exe)
  28. tg-macos-amd64-cpu was built on an Intel macOS runner label, currently macos-15-intel
  29. includes required package-manager bundle assets (tensor-grep.rb, oimiragieo.tensor-grep.yaml, PUBLISH_INSTRUCTIONS.md)
  30. includes CHECKSUMS.txt and BUNDLE_CHECKSUMS.txt parity validation
  31. Confirm terminal publish gate is green:
  32. normal semantic-release path: publish-success-gate
  33. manual/backfill tag path: release-success-gate (parity + npm publish + docs deploy)
  34. includes final registry parity re-checks before success confirmation
  35. Verify published version parity:
  36. GitHub tag version equals PyPI latest version
  37. GitHub tag version equals npm/package.json version
  38. npm registry latest equals X.Y.Z (verified by release workflow parity step)

docs.title: 4. Package-manager distribution finalization
docs.text:
Detailed operational steps live in docs/package_manager_publish.md.

  1. Homebrew formula readiness:
  2. CI runs ruby -c scripts/tensor-grep.rb.
  3. Ensure formula URL points at https://github.com/oimiragieo/tensor-grep/releases/download/v#{version}/....
  4. Winget manifest readiness:
  5. CI runs winget validate on Windows when available and falls back to Python validator only when validation is unavailable, or when hosted-runner winget reports only the known schema-header URL warning and the stricter Python release-asset validator also passes.
  6. Ensure PackageLocale, PackageVersion, nested Installers[0].InstallerUrl, and Installers[0].InstallerSha256 in scripts/oimiragieo.tensor-grep.yaml are schema-valid for the current release.
  7. Release bundle generation stamps Installers[0].InstallerSha256 from generated artifacts/CHECKSUMS.txt before upload.
  8. CI also builds artifacts/package-manager-bundle and verifies BUNDLE_CHECKSUMS.txt parity in package-manager-readiness.
  9. CI uploads package-manager-bundle-<os> artifacts for operator inspection/download from each green run.
  10. Main CI preflights package-manager bundle generation/verification/smoke checks in package-manager-readiness before semantic-release starts.
  11. Post-release operational publish:
  12. Homebrew tap update: open/update PR in tap repo with new formula.
  13. Winget submission: create/update manifest PR in winget-pkgs for new version.
  14. Keep release artifacts canonical:
  15. Build artifacts must map 1:1 to tag version and expected filenames.
  16. Main CI builds release-native CPU front-door binaries from the semantic-release tag only when semantic-release reports released == true, smoke-runs --version/--help, and renames them to the installer URLs.
  17. Non-release main pushes must not reuse the current package version to upload assets to the previous GitHub release.
  18. publish-github-release-assets validates the expected native-front-door filename matrix and emits CHECKSUMS.txt (SHA256) before uploading GitHub release assets.
  19. publish-github-release-assets also generates and publishes package-manager bundle assets (Homebrew formula + Winget manifest + instructions) for repeatable downstream submission.
  20. publish-github-release-assets runs both bundle integrity and content smoke checks before publish:
    • scripts/verify_package_manager_bundle_checksums.py --bundle-dir artifacts/package-manager-bundle
    • scripts/smoke_test_package_manager_bundle.py --bundle-dir artifacts/package-manager-bundle

docs.title: 5. Rollback runbook
docs.text:
Use this when a bad release escaped:

  1. Stop forward publishes:
  2. Temporarily disable release workflow or merge a hotfix with skip release in commit message.
  3. If PyPI publication is incorrect:
  4. Publish a patch release with corrected contents (preferred).
  5. Do not rely on deleting artifacts as a primary rollback mechanism.
  6. If GitHub release assets are incorrect:
  7. Rebuild artifacts for the correct tag.
  8. Replace assets in GitHub release and rerun validators.
  9. Package manager rollback:
  10. Homebrew: revert formula in tap to previous known-good version.
  11. Winget: submit manifest update pointing to previous known-good installer.
  12. Incident close-out:
  13. Add root cause + mitigation to CHANGELOG.md and the relevant public technical guide (if architecture-impacting).
  14. Add/adjust CI assertion so the specific failure cannot recur.

docs.title: 6. Operator verification commands
docs.text:
# CI + release status
gh run list --limit 10

# Quick version parity checks
python - << 'PY'
import tomllib, json
from pathlib import Path
print("pyproject:", tomllib.loads(Path("pyproject.toml").read_text())["project"]["version"])
print("cargo:", [l for l in Path("rust_core/Cargo.toml").read_text().splitlines() if l.startswith("version = ")][0])
print("npm:", json.loads(Path("npm/package.json").read_text())["version"])
PY

# Release asset consistency
uv run python scripts/validate_release_assets.py
python scripts/verify_github_release_assets.py --repo oimiragieo/tensor-grep --tag vX.Y.Z

docs.title: Support matrix
docs.text: As of 2026-10-06, this page separates tested build environments from published install channels and best-effort use. CI coverage means a workflow exercises that platform; it does not mean the newest run is green or guarantee every machine configuration.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text:
Platform Evidence and practical limits Linux x64 Main CI tests Linux builds. A CPU native release asset is published. Other glibc-compatible distributions are best-effort and depend on compatibility with that asset and the Python dependencies. Windows x64 Main CI tests Windows builds. A CPU native release asset is published. Windows Server variants are best-effort and are not separately exhaustive. macOS x64 Native build and CPU release asset are covered by release workflows. macOS arm64 (Apple Silicon) CI provides native build coverage, but there is no arm64 release asset in the current published CPU asset set. Use a supported Python install or build from source; the x64 asset under Rosetta is another operator-managed option.

The default native asset profile is CPU. The CI workflow has a separate native-frontdoor-gpu profile that gates GPU asset build steps; that profile is not the default release profile. GPU support is experimental and depends on build options, compatible hardware, drivers, and the route actually selected. See experimental features and the GPU runbook.

docs.title: Python and Rust versions
docs.text:
• Python package floor: Python 3.11 or newer (pyproject.toml declares >=3.11).
  • Python versions exercised by the documented CI matrix: 3.11 and 3.12.
  • Python < 3.11 is unsupported.
  • Rust maintainers should use the stable toolchain specified by CI and release workflows. The source manifest's minimum toolchain is not a promise that every older stable compiler can reproduce current release builds.

docs.title: Published channels
docs.text: PyPI, GitHub Release CPU binaries, and their managed install scripts are the available user channels described by installation. npm/npx, Homebrew, and Winget manifests exist in the repository but are not published to their registries. Do not interpret CI validation of a manifest as registry availability.

docs.title: Compatibility and support policy
docs.text:
tensor-grep follows Semantic Versioning. Minor releases add features compatibly; major releases may change CLI flags, configuration, or machine-readable outputs. The detailed compatibility rules live in contracts.

Stable features, flags, and fields scheduled for removal are marked DEPRECATED for at least 90 days and 2 minor versions, whichever period is longer. The time floor matters because multiple minor releases can occur close together.

Only the latest released version receives security fixes. There are no maintenance branches or older supported lines; upgrades carry fixes forward. Version-pinned or air-gapped deployments should account for that policy.

Experimental features are outside stable compatibility guarantees and may change in a minor release. Their current setup and limits are listed in Experimental features.

docs.title: Agent outcome join
docs.text: benchmarks/agent_outcome_join.py joins benchmark predictions to observed patch execution.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
A join is authorized ONLY by the full tuple: system_id, instance_id, repo_commit, tool_version, model_id, budget_id.

A record missing any field is never completed by guessing. It appears in unidentified_predictions / unidentified_outcomes with the exact missing_fields list. Duplicate full identities fail closed on both sides: neither row joins, and the pair is reported in duplicate_identities.

docs.title: Command fit is not success
docs.text:
command_fit means a validation command was PLANNED. verified_task_success requires an observed passing execution bound to the same identity:

execution_observed validation_passed outcome_state counted in denominator? true true passed yes true false failed yes false anything unavailable no

verified_task_success_rate divides by complete_cases (observed executions only) and is null when that count is zero. Zero evidence is never reported as success.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: tokens_in/tokens_out/elapsed_s include failed attempts. If any joined row is missing a cost value, the corresponding total is null, not zero.

docs.title: Legacy records
docs.text: adapt_legacy_bakeoff_row maps a run_patch_bakeoff.py result row (instance_id + system) onto the outcome shape. It supplies system_id from system, derives execution_observed from patch_applied, and defaults the three cost fields to null; it does not invent the four remaining identity fields, so the record remains unidentified by design. Legacy readers and existing recall metrics are unchanged -- this module adds a report, it does not modify any existing one.

docs.title: Where the report will be emitted
docs.text: A consumer could embed the report under the top-level outcome_join key of the scorecard artifact written by build_external_agent_patch_driver_scorecard.py. No consumer exists yet: this slice defines and verifies build_outcome_join_report, but currently emits its output nowhere.

docs.title: Not covered
docs.text: This module does not establish end-to-end benchmark success. Holdout curation is not implemented here; it remains a separate follow-up that requires real repository fixtures and known-good patches.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: tensor-grep (tg) has a Rust command-line program and a Python package. Which one receives a command first depends on how the user installed it. The command names are designed to feel like one tool, but the two installation entry points do not have identical startup and dependency paths.

docs.title: Follow a request
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  U[User or tool] --> F{Installed front door}
  F -->|Managed native binary| R[Rust CLI]
  F -->|Python package| P[Python CLI]
  P -->|Eligible delegated command| R
  R -->|Text search| S{Selected engine}
  S --> RG[rg, when eligible]
  S --> CPU[Native CPU]
  S --> IDX[Trigram index]
  S --> GPU[Optional GPU route]
  R -->|Python-backed command| SIDE[Managed Python sidecar]
  R -->|tg run AST path| AST[AST workflow]
  P --> AST
  P --> OTHER[Python command or backend]

The diagram is a map, not a complete routing specification. Some commands have early passthrough paths, and tg run has an AST path. The maintained conditions are in routing policy.

docs.title: The two installation entry points
docs.text:
• Managed native install: the released native binary is the tg front door. It handles native text search and can hand Python-backed commands to the managed Python sidecar. A sidecar is a separate process used to provide commands implemented in Python.
  • Python package install: the console command starts through Python. It can use packaged Rust extensions for supported native functionality, and some features that require a standalone executable need an explicitly configured native binary.

Within the Rust executable, both the bare positional search form (tg PATTERN PATH) and command form (tg search PATTERN PATH) can lead to the text-search router. These are two parser forms inside one binary; they are separate from the native-versus-Python installation choice. tg run follows an AST workflow path. Do not infer the implementation for a command from its name alone; see the route details for current behavior.

docs.title: Search engines and limits
docs.text:
The search router can select rg, native CPU search, a trigram index, an AST backend, or optional GPU paths according to flags, output shape, available tools, and project state. A backend is the engine that performs the request. Routing is conditional, so a release containing a GPU-related build configuration does not mean GPU is the default or that every search uses it.

The trigram index records character groups to narrow which files need a full scan. It is a file named .tg_index at the indexed project root. It can narrow some compatible text searches; whether it is used depends on the query and route. For exact flags and fallbacks, use routing policy.

AST workflows parse source into an abstract syntax tree (AST), then match or analyze code structure. Parser and language coverage constrain what can be found. Call graphs and caller lists can have unresolved or bounded results, so an absent edge is not proof that no caller exists. Orientation scores suggest central files or entry points from available signals; they are not proof of runtime importance or safety.

docs.title: From a question to relevant code
docs.text:
Commands such as tg context and tg prepare use Python services to gather and rank candidate files and symbols. A symbol is a named code element, such as a function or class. Query words, symbol matches, filenames, and relationships between code elements help select useful results. Production files, tests, generated code, and vendored code can receive different treatment. Exact symbol evidence takes priority over a filename phrase match.

The selected results must fit an output budget. This makes them practical to read or send to an assistant, but it also means that relevant code may be omitted. Sessions reuse project snapshots for repeated requests; refreshing a session updates its view after files change. Ranking and caching do not establish that a proposed edit is correct.

docs.title: CLI and MCP access
docs.text:
People can read command output in a terminal. Scripts can request structured JSON or NDJSON where supported. MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets a compatible assistant call the tool's search and analysis functions through tg mcp. These interfaces share underlying services, while their public input and output contracts are documented in the harness API. Running an MCP server does not by itself grant a client permission to apply every proposed change.

By default, tg mcp starts a server exposing 58 tools. The registered tool list is the source of truth; clients can discover it through MCP, and the API reference describes the available operations.

docs.title: Local state has different purposes
docs.text:
Location Purpose How to treat it .tg_index Native trigram index file used by eligible text searches Rebuildable search data; may be removed when the index is stale .tg_cache/ast/ AST project data, including project_data_v6.json Rebuildable parser and project data; separate from the text index .tensor-grep/sessions/ Persisted session metadata and snapshots State for reusable project context; inspect before cleanup .tensor-grep/checkpoints/ Saved file contents and metadata for rollback Durable recovery material; do not delete when clearing caches Resident worker memory Optional in-process AST data Volatile; worker behavior is experimental

Some session requests may use an optional daemon response cache. That cache is scoped to daemon requests and is not the checkpoint store. See cache management before removing local state and session daemon protocol for session behavior.

docs.title: Persisted semantic index library
docs.text:
src/tensor_grep/core/semantic_index.py is retained as a library-only component. Its build_and_save and load_or_warn APIs persist chunk-BM25 data under .tg_semantic_index/ (bm25_chunks.json and bm25_meta.json). This store is separate from the native trigram .tg_index and the AST project cache.

The persisted semantic index is not wired into production CLI, MCP, or session requests. There is no tg index command for this store; tg search --rank ranks in memory. Keeping the library does not promise persisted acceleration for those commands, and the absence of an in-repository caller does not establish that an exported library API is unused by downstream applications.

Loads check the schema, chunker mode, and a fingerprint over sorted source paths and modification times. A mismatch warns and returns None so callers can choose an in-memory fallback rather than serve stale data. The library's corpus is not size-capped; applications must bound input when they need a resource limit.

docs.title: Source map
docs.text: Area Role rust_core/ Native CLI, text-search routing, indexing, and native execution paths src/tensor_grep/cli/ Python command handlers and CLI workflows src/tensor_grep/backends/ Backend interfaces and implementations src/tensor_grep/core/ Shared Python core logic tests/ Tests for command contracts and behavior scripts/ Build, release, validation, and maintenance tools

docs.title: Contracts and implementation detail
docs.text: Contracts is the canonical source for compatibility promises, completeness fields, state behavior, and failure semantics. Harness API documents machine-readable output. Experimental features identifies behavior outside stable guarantees. This overview intentionally avoids duplicating the full routing table and contract ledger.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: tensor-grep is designed as a routing-first search engine that keeps strict behavioral parity while selecting the best backend per query class.
